This paper presents a novel approach to reconstructing 4D scenes using neural learning from limited views. A key innovation of our method is the use of geometric constraints to refine the estimated geometry. We demonstrate that incorporating these constraints significantly improves the accuracy of scene geometry reconstruction while also enabling the estimation of unknown view positions. Our geometric constraints are integrated into a variational framework along with a data-fitting term for optimal position estimation. A neural network is then utilized to enforce the estimated geometry, thereby improving position accuracy. Notably, our method enables the learning of 4D scenes using a sparse and limited view dataset, such as that obtained from only two views. A novel geometric constraint is developed to accurately reconstruct a missing view while leveraging position estimation and 2D alignment. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through successful reconstruction of 4D scenes from sparse and limited views, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in the process.

Between 2019 and 2020, speckle interferometry observations were conducted at the ASTELLA2 telescope at the Observatorio Astron\'omico Nacional de Almer\'ia, spanning a total of 170 nights. These observations utilized the BICOR beam-combination technique and covered a period of time spanning 620 days. A total of 725 measurements were made, resulting in the acquisition of 725 speckle spectra, out of which 716 were successfully combined to yield high precision astrometric data for 343 stellar systems. By analyzing these data, along with existing parallax information, it was possible to determine the 3D motion of many stellar systems, including several previously unknown systems. Moreover, it was found that some binary and multiple star systems were closer to being in alignment than previously thought. A total of 234 new pairs or subsystems were identified, along with 43 newly discovered multiple systems, bringing the total number of observed systems to 343. These data sets have been made available online through the Speckle Observations of Relative InfraRed (SORIR) database.

We're studying the structure of a specific mathematical series called operator-product expansions in Self-Dual (SD) gravity and N=8 superconformal theory in six dimensions. Our findings show how the series' structure connects to the associativity of the theory's operators, which in turn influences the overall structure of scattering amplitudes. By utilizing the series' chiral properties, we developed a system to compute and verify the series' higher-order terms. The research also involved developing a customized representation of the series based on a specific type of contractions and using the series' causal properties to derive constraints on the coefficients of the higher-order terms. The results of the research further validated the series' higher-order terms using known data on supergravity scattering amplitudes in eleven dimensions.

A newly identified shock front in three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations accelerates a sinusoidal solar jet, creating a fundamental frequency and its harmonic shock front. The shock accelerates at the expense of the solar jet's kinetic energy, reaching speeds around 160 km/s per year relative to the jet. The shock's speed is dominated by its frame of reference, exceeding the solar jet speed of 13.5 km/s. The modeled shock resembles the physical shock studied in observations and spectroscopy of a type II radio burst associated with a solar jet, Steven's Quasar. The relative shock speed surpasses the solar jet speed by an order of magnitude, indicating the shock may drive the jet's instability and its associated radio burst.

We have analyzed potential future collider experiments within the widely accepted general two Higgs doublet model in light of upcoming B meson decay observations and research into alleged lepton flavor violations. Our findings suggest that future colliders will be capable of detecting signature patterns from this model that appear in both type-II and type-IV Higgs doublet scenarios, such as a mass peak around 125 GeV, its characteristics in production and decay, its properties and relationships, its interactions with gauge bosons, the top quark, and the W and Z bosons. We particularly note that the general two Higgs doublet model can account for the observed mass of the observed Higgs boson without contradicting recent experimental results from the LHC. We have also made explicit predictions for future collider experiments based on a specific benchmark scenario, the general two Higgs doublet model in which one Higgs doublet largely escapes detection at colliders while the other contributes substantially to the production of the observed Higgs boson. We have determined the expected mass and production rates for several hypothetical particles including CP-odd particles, CP-even particles, and charged particles as well as the predicted rates for various processes including charged particle associated production, charged particle decay into the observed Higgs boson, charged particle decay into the observed Higgs boson accompanied by other particles, and the production and decay of hypothetical particles.

We introduce a novel numerical technique for solving three-dimensional fluid flow equations by adapting techniques successfully applied in two-dimensional dynamics. A new model, random vortex dynamics, is developed specifically for use on grids with uniform Chladni patterns and is designed to mimic the behavior of vortices on the surface of a sphere. This approach can reduce computational complexity by eliminating the need for explicit numerical solving of the Navier-Stokes equations on a sphere's grid, ultimately speeding up the computational process. To validate this method's effectiveness, we compare it with the standard shallow water model and find that it yields results comparable to high-order spectral methods on coarser grids, yet offers significantly higher computational efficiency.

Quantum information theories can describe both fully photonic systems and those incorporating phonons, where the phonons act as a environment for photonic modes. By examining the entanglement between a subsystem and its environment, we find that the entanglement ratio approaches 1 as the size of the subsystem approaches the number of photons, whether photonic or photonic-phononic. This limiting behavior is an indicator that the entanglement cannot be directly quantified using the subsystem's reduced density operator. Our analysis also reveals that the logarithmic negativity in a subsystem-Environment pair follows a random matrix theory prediction, which diverges as the environment size approaches infinity. This outcome is an inherent property of all qudit systems not protected by conservation laws and is experimentally observable in the continuous variable setting.

Relevance learning plays a significant role in reducing computational complexity and enhance the efficiency of systems that identify predictive variables from time-series data. For high-throughput time-dependent expression analysis, Relevance learning accelerates search processes, such as those applied in gene finding, regulatory discovery, and genome-scale modeling. A new method called REGEN was developed to efficiently identify co-regulated genes. Combining relevance learning with an optimized sequence alignment algorithm, REGEN detects significant co-regulated genes within seconds for large genomic datasets. According to evaluations using 12 yeast and bacterial datasets, REGEN outperformed existing methods in both speed and accuracy, demonstrating a strong correlation between regulatory distances and statistical results. Additionally, the expression levels of co-regulated genes were found to be influenced by a smaller number of variables, as compared to those without such regulation, exemplified by the analysis using the yeast pheromone response network, where the co-regulated genes, including ELU1, SSN8, and PRM3, were found to be dependent on only 22 variables out of 6451 genes, in contrast to the co-regulated genes, including GAL4, being dependent on 41 variables.

In the field of control systems, we compare the predicted state of a system with the internal state of a specially designed recurrent neural network. This neural network is trained to mimic the system state by learning from past data. We prove a mathematical equivalence between the neural network's hidden state and the beliefs of a system state, which are derived from an optimal control approach for partially observable environments. Additionally, we establish that the neural network's output approximates the control signal, and we determine the conditions under which the neural network's predictions will not exceed the true system state.

Our proposed framework, ACTS, is comprised of two key components: self-attention processing for video action understanding and Graph Convolutional Networking for semantic relation mapping. By integrating global video semantic information through self-attention processing, ACTS achieves an understanding of key action features. Simultaneously, it utilizes GCN to establish the semantic connection between action features and action classes, representing action recognition as a graph-based problem rather than a traditional pipeline. This unique approach enables ACTS to capture the complex and distinctive features of actions, particularly in low-quality video scenarios. Our results demonstrate ACTS achieving superior performance on the MINC and Charades datasets, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods by about 1% accuracy without employing pre-training or online end-to-action features derived from temporal action proposals.

This research introduces a novel solution to the image copy detection problem.
The proposed method combines features commonly used in similar applications,
including bag-of-words, bag-of-visual-words with descriptors, and bag-of-
regions with soft descriptors, allowing it to leverage diverse information.
Experimental results demonstrate the method's capabilities on the widely used
CUB-200-2011 and Stanford Online Product datasets, showcasing performance
comparable to state-of-the-art approaches with the potential to enhance current
best practices.

The well-posedness for a certain class of initial-boundary value problems involving the Laplace and heat equations under Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions is studied. These problems are characterized by a coefficient defined within a Besov space on a specific domain. Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions give rise to distinct heat equations, with Dirichlet conditions involving the trace operator and Neumann conditions involving the potential operator. We establish well-posedness for all three equations while employing a coherent approach that highlights the connections between these results. Furthermore, this analysis also covers the stability of the inverse problems associated with the heat equation, with the coefficient being semi-smooth and semi-continuous, with the former condition implying the latter.

This study explores the thermodynamic properties of neutron stars composed of nuclear matter at zero temperature without magnetic field constraints using the Cranking Skyrmme interaction, a minimally viable ErPMS, within the context of Relativistic Mean Field Theory. The investigation focuses on energy density and pressure, as well as spin polarization, with both analytically and numerically calculated energy and pressure being divisible by 4, indicating a residual symmetry at zero temperature without magnetic field, as per QCD requirements. Moreover, spin polarization is discovered to be a function of both energy density and pressure, with a calculated spin polarization of 0.5 at saturation density, reflecting a quark-like nature of nuclear matter at this density. With a total neutron star mass of 2 solar masses, the research finds analytically derived pressures and energies, as well as a calculated binding energy, energy density, and pressure at the center of a neutron star, with a negative binding energy of -2.0372 times the rest energy per baryon at the center of a 2 solar mass neutron star, similar to quark matter, causing a small oscillation in the pressure and energy of the neutron star, with a maximum variation of 0.22 and 0.65, respectively, at the center of a 2 solar mass neutron star, with further investigation into the pressure and energy oscillation boundaries revealed through numerical calculations, showing a maximum variation of 0.55 and 1.55, respectively

Federated learning's renowned compression-driven efficiency, which minimizes the transmission amount while maintaining accuracy, has significant ecological and security implications.  However, conventional methods of compression, such as quantization, are not in line with the differential privacy concept.  This research presents the first compression approach based on differential privacy, aimed at addressing this issue.  A general framework for differential private compression is developed, and two specific methods, individual label differential privacy and group-based label differential privacy, are introduced.  Furthermore, the study examines and analyzes the differential private compression of Gaussian distribution and its application to federated learning, providing a basis for future research into this area.

The far-ultraviolet intensity observed in the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex is largely attributed to the molecular hydrogen within the complex, with supplemental radiation coming from a few identified UV-bright sources. Analyzing the combined hydrogen and known source intensities reveals that the complex's far-ultraviolet intensity meets the necessary standards to nurture a vast array of sub-stellar objects. Furthermore, this analysis is consistent with a phenomenon known as "cosmic ray diffusion," where galactic cosmic rays regulate the formation of these objects. Notably, by examining a vast sample of 35 complexes, our research indicates that the hydrogen intensity in complexes like Taurus-Auriga-Perseus is 2 to 4 times more elevated than expected, suggesting an external factor is increasing the far-ultraviolet intensity, potentially facilitating the formation of sub-stellar objects.

Extracting table information from documents is a critical step in information processing, crucial for subsequent tasks like data entry, search, and citation reference identification. Advances in machine learning have made Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) well-suited to handle the complexities of document images. Our proposed framework combines GNNs with Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to enhance the accuracy of table extraction and overall structure understanding. By focusing on detection, extraction, and format normalization of tables, our method leverages a flexible, patch-based graph representation that allows GNNs to capture the interconnections between pixels, tables, and their contents. Our framework's adaptability also enables the incorporation of external information, ensemble learning, and semi-supervised settings. Experimental results show significant improvements over current state-of-the-art methods on the IIIT dataset, yielding a 2.5% increase in extraction accuracy.

In the game of Noughts and Crosses, participants take turns playing against each other across a 4x4 grid. The player who creates three identical symbols in a row, column, or diagonal wins. Researchers at Oxford University studied the strategy of this game through a survey of 317 university students who played against each other. Each participant kept a record of their own wins, draws, and losses. The analysis showed that lower-level students (who were under 20 years old) tended to adopt an aggressive strategy, making their best move each turn and occasionally mistaking the outcome of their actions. Higher-level students (who were 21 or older) exhibited a more nuanced approach, recognizing that their opponents were also strategic players. The research suggests that lower-level students had a superficial understanding of the game while higher-level students had developed a deeper perspective, incorporating probability and opponent analysis to inform their decisions. The study's findings are based on an analysis of the game outcomes, which revealed significant differences in wins, draws, and losses between the two groups.

Predicting the user base of an app is crucial for investors and entrepreneurs, involving an analysis of available features such as ARPU, app store ratings, and reviews. However, apps provide additional data including user footprint maps, GPS trail records, and device metadata. Existing studies have explored the potential of geospatial analysis in app prediction but most methods are proprietary and lack public evaluation. This paper assesses a range of publicly accessible features including footprint area estimation to enhance population predictions. Results indicate that incorporating footprint area estimation significantly improves forecast accuracy, with an improvement of 8% over sole public feature use. Code for the analysis is available on the platform for reproducibility and open-source development.

A novel, static filtering technique has been devised to counteract the limitations of false positives while preserving network throughput, efficiency, and speed. This innovative method integrates a predefined set of rules into a single, powerful device that processes incoming traffic, allowing it to efficiently forward packets and maintain performance comparable to state-of-the-art systems. Furthermore, a modular architecture variant of the technique has been proposed to enhance its flexibility and scalability for real-world applications.

We have developed an anisotropic non-rigid pendulum model to describe a recently discovered phenomenon where real-time observation causes an instability in a quantum system. This phenomenon, referred to as the quantum wave function collapse rule, leads to rapid atom-molecule conversions and is accurately represented by our model. By analyzing the model's dynamics, we have identified two modes of motion and found that its behavior closely resembles that of a damped harmonic oscillator near its tipping point. Using these insights and a wave function approximation approach, we have derived an effective theory that describes the model's dynamics and provides valuable physical insights into this phenomenon, including its ability to trigger instabilities and influence ring-down times. We have also validated our theory by comparing its predictions with high-quality simulations and experiments. Notably, our research has demonstrated that even small interactions between individual atoms can lead to significant dynamics and phenomena, such as atom-molecule phase transitions, and we have discussed its potential applications in exploring novel phases of matter.

The proposed multi-phase SPH model in this research is designed to address phase-related issues within multi-resolution SPH methods. By introducing mass and momentum conserving phase functions, the model effectively eliminates artifacts resulting from high-density ratios and phase separation. A two-phase model was implemented and tested on three cases: Saffman Taylor problem, bubble dynamics, and solidifying alloy solidification. Saffman-Taylor problem simulations showed accurate and convergent results for both phases. Further simulations of bursting bubbles and solidifying alloy solidification demonstrated the model's ability to handle complex two-phase flows and solidification processes. Notably, the model's ability to achieve single-particle precision in mass conservation was demonstrated.

A popular clustering method, K-means, has seen quantum enhancements in recent years. The initial quantum K-means algorithm was developed by Beigi and Amini, followed by optimizations by Brassard and others. This paper presents a new quantum K-means algorithm that outperforms all previous versions by reducing the number of qubit measurements needed to solve the problem. The proposed algorithm specifically resolves it in O(np^2 log(p)) expected repetitions, where n is the total number of data points and p the number of clusters. While some existing algorithms achieve a similar expected measure of success with fewer queries to an oracle, they necessitate more queries on average, leading to an increased computational expense. Another advantage of this algorithm is its capacity to handle data points with multiple features (n > 1) using a quantum parallelization approach, a limitation in all prior algorithms.

Utilizing large speech datasets with pitch variations can be costly and labor-intensive to annotate. The level of pitch controllability in existing datasets may not meet current standards of speech synthesis models. This study investigates the effectiveness of incorporating pitch-augmented datasets during unsupervised speech synthesis training. By combining multiple datasets with the same transcription but varying pitch, the model achieves enhanced pitch controllability. We demonstrate that utilizing pitch correction alignment (PCA) greatly improves pitch control quality. The proposed approach was evaluated using the LJS001, LJS002, and MJSynth datasets, with the results indicating a significant improvement in pitch quality and control. Furthermore, it was observed that including datasets with extreme pitch values can lead to increased pitch range in the synthesized speech.

Object-centric understanding, long considered a hallmark of human intelligence, has gained significant traction in machine learning. This research delves into spatiotemporal object-centric reasoning through a new self-supervised learning framework, known as Contrastive Spatiotemporal Object Learning (CSOL). By employing a contrastive loss, CSOL fosters a representation where objects with the same identity are more closely related across space and time. CSOL operates without relying on annotated object data, instead utilizing automatic object detection to create labels for pre-trained models. This method can adapt to various object detection tools and model backbones, including those with pre-trained image-based features. CSOL's efficacy was evaluated using two spatiotemporal object-centric benchmarks, ATOP-50B and ATOP-R-48, developed specifically for this purpose. Results indicate that CSOL yields superior performance on these benchmarks, outperforming both baseline models as well as state-of-the-art object tracking models. Moreover, CSOL-derived representations demonstrate robustness across different tasks, including image-based object classification.

The ALEPH group within the ATLAS Cocktails Collaboration extensively studied
lepton pair production off-light, off-muons, and off-electrons, utilizing the
ATLAS detector's simulations to compare with current CC DY measurements.
Our analysis focused on charged-current Drell-Yan observables, including the
transverse-momentum distribution of lepton pairs, to assess the simulation
accuracy. This work shows that the simulation precision for this specific
observable is around 5%, which is comparable to previous studies for other
observables. This level of precision is crucial for further investigations. For
example, such a study could be extended to compare the simulation's predicted
lepton-pair distributions with data from the 2015 and 2016 LHC runs.

This study is the first to delve into how Telepresence Robot users rate their overall experience. To gauge these ratings, we conducted two distinct studies. Firstly, we surveyed existing TR users to understand their overall experience and pinpoint the key factors contributing to it. Secondly, we recruited novices to operate a TR and asked them to compare their overall experience with two distinct approaches: one where they experienced a virtual environment and another where they operated the TR. The results showed that TR users value both visual and navigational aspects equally when operating the system, yet novices place greater importance on visual elements due to increased distraction. Additionally, we discovered that TR navigation/control is only crucial when users are engaged with the activity, not when they are socially interacting.

The analysis of whole-plant morphology in relation to nutrient soil concentration has traditionally been examined through allometric scaling rules, yet these empirical relationships may also result from mechanistic processes. We aim to understand how a simple plant growth model, based on an optimisation process, connects with allometric relations in a whole-plant context. This plant growth model links plant size to soil nutrient concentration, allowing for the identification of two distinct hierarchical patterns. One pattern follows a linear relationship, similar to isometric growth, and can be achieved by an optimal balance between mass accumulation and stem elongation. Another pattern, resembling a power-law relationship, arises from balancing these two factors against whole-plant length. Our findings reveal that plant models with optimal and self-critical growth mechanisms can replicate both geometric relationships between plant and soil characteristics, without the need for differential equations that model growth dynamics explicitly.

Mafia is a well-liked social deduction game involving interpersonal interactions, where players can be innocent individuals or hidden mafia members with the goal of eliminating innocent players. This study treats Mafia as a multi-stage game of imperfect information where players make decisions about killing and lynching, and we provide a mathematical framework to model the game. Notably, the complexity and uncertainty inherent in the game stem from its nonstationarity, unmarkovian dynamics, and the inability to determine other players' true status or future actions with certainty. By examining the likelihood of lynching innocent individuals and eliminating the mafia threat, we explore the conditions necessary for innocent players to ultimately triumph. This approach enables us to identify key factors influencing the game's outcome and provide insights on how to increase the chances of success.

Accumulating evidence suggests gas giants with similar masses in hierarchical multiple systems coalesce from the same disk, implying a need for a mechanism that synchronizes the accretion process. We introduce two dynamical mechanisms capable of reducing the mass difference between multiple giant planets accumulating from the same disk. By perturbing the disk, these mechanisms facilitate a smooth, efficient, and nearly simultaneous accretion process for multiple planets. Past studies have shown similar results for disks of up to 5 planets in different configurations, highlighting the importance of considering the long-term dynamics of accretion disk gas giants.

The electrical conductivity of a film made from armchair single-wall carbon nanotubes was investigated and measured in both heat and cold temperatures. The high-temperature conductivity was found to be largely due to electrical current percolation through a film of individual carbon nanotubes that were entangled with each other. However, the low-temperature conductivity was discovered to be significantly influenced by electronic spin interference caused by carbon nanotubes that were in close proximity to one another, which resulted in a large and temperature-dependent increase in electrical conductivity. This interference caused by nearby carbon nanitubes was found to significantly enhance the low-temperature conductivity of the carbon nanotube film. The observation of a large and temperature-dependent low-temperature conductivity provides strong evidence for the spin-Hamiltonian nature of electronic transport in low-synclinal single-wall carbon nanotubes, which occurs through a transfer of electronic waves between carbon atoms that are in close proximity to one another. The results also suggest that the low-temperature conductivity of entangled single-wall carbon nanotube films can be fine-tuned by varying the concentration of carbon nanotubes that are in close proximity to one another.

Several types of fuzzy k-means clustering methods have been proposed to deal with data points of multiple membership degrees. However, a common issue among these methods is the overfitting problem that occurs when the number of clusters is set to a small value. To address this problem, we present a novel objective function for fuzzy k-means clustering, incorporating an entropy term to relax the constraints of traditional methods. The performance of the proposed approach is evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its effectiveness in mitigating overfitting. The experiments demonstrate that the membership degrees generated by this method adhere to a soft interval, thereby improving the quality of the clustering results.

We've devised a novel algorithm for determining the parameters of a mixture-of-experts model based on unlabeled data. Unlike traditional algorithms reliant on maximum likelihood estimation, our approach yields highly accurate estimates of expert weights, mixing weights, and output dimensions. By contrast, our algorithm outperforms previous research, achieving estimates of expert weights within 1% of their true values. We've also applied this algorithm to a range of real-world tasks, including handwritten digit recognition, where it successfully identified varying output formats among a batch of images.

The study of Jacobians and Prym varieties is a fundamental area of research in algebraic geometry, with important applications in geometry and physics. Building on previous work in this field, the notes examine how the geometry of the Jacobian and Prym spaces change under the action of symplectomorphisms, with a particular focus on the impact of the Campana-Pogodalevich conjecture. To investigate the more complex structures of Prym varieties, the notes begin by revisiting the basic properties of Prym varieties and their tangent bundles, before using the Campana-Pogodalevich conjecture to analyze the symplectic geometry of the Prym space and its quasismall deformations.

We establish a theoretical framework that encapsulates gravity's impact on global symmetries, deriving a quantifiable restriction on the breaking of global symmetries imposed by gravity. This boundary condition encompasses various gravity theories, including Einstein's, and is applicable to quantum theories of gravity that conform to quantum general relativity and accommodate matter. The breaking of global symmetries is directly linked to a measure of gravitational deformation. Considering two prominent theories of quantum gravity, where matter is described by string theory and the spin foam model, these formulations adhere to the boundary condition, signifying that all deformations can be quantified and made infinitesimally small. Consequently, this boundary condition has far-reaching implications for the development of effective field theories. Specifically, it validates the concept of global symmetries at multiple scales and solidifies the validity of well-established effective field theories. Furthermore, it ensures that gravity's influence does not contradict conservation laws, thereby solidifying the principles of well-established effective field theories.

Our research presents findings from an investigation into the blue horizontal branch (BHB) sequence of the globular cluster M13. Through the application of the general starstrumpet tool, we used Gaia DR2 and DRV data to identify distinct sub-populations within the cluster's BHB. Gaia DR2 data allowed us to pinpoint ten BHB stars, while Gaia DRV data enabled the detection of five first-ascent blue ridge (FABR) and twelve blue horizontal branch stars. Analyzing the Gaia DR2 luminosity and color distributions led to the classification of four distinct BHB sub-populations. FABR analysis revealed two sub-populations. Our results indicate the presence of multiple sub-populations within M13, consistent with previous studies on the cluster's double blue horizontal branch phenomenon.

The 1989 Madsen-Weiss theorem ties together three key topological concepts: the Madsen-Weiss theorem itself, a specific stability theorem arising from the Madsen-Weiss theorem, and Euler's characteristic from the point of view of the b-principle. We propose a broader interpretation that extends beyond the core scenario of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, applying to various other boundary components in the Madsen-Weiss type. This expanded framework leads to novel generalizations, including one that aligns with the universal coherent orientation principle suggested by Farb-Madsen and Lee. We also outline general approaches to proving the underlying homotopy type stability, as well as a conjecture related to the characteristic numbers of boundary components, which builds upon earlier work by Galatius-Leinster and Madsen-Weiss.

A key concept in the study of neural network knowledge transfer is the idea of 'transferable knowledge', which refers to the capacity of a pre-trained network to apply skills or learn new tasks. Research has demonstrated that different layers of a neural network exhibit varying degrees of knowledge transferability. Typically, the topmost layers of a network are considered non-robust knowledge sources as they are highly specialized in identity mapping. However, recent findings have challenged this notion by revealing that the output activations of the topmost layers of pre-trained networks can serve as effective transferable knowledge sources. This study proposes a novel explanation for this counterintuitive phenomenon by showing that the output activations of the topmost layers of a neural network are characterized by low entropy, which makes them susceptible to adversarial attacks. Furthermore, we establish that the output activations of all network layers are transferable by developing a novel theoretical framework based on mutual information. Using the established framework, we investigate the knowledge transferability of the output activations of individual neurons, demonstrating that they too can serve as a transferable knowledge source.

We examine the dynamics of information spread through a study of seed-based activation on various network architectures. Starting with a given set of active nodes, we aim to explore how the optimal network configuration relates to information diffusion parameters. Our research indicates that at an optimal network design, the seed size and target propagation size are equal, resulting in minimum exerted effort. Focusing on scale-free networks, where nodes by nature have varying connection probabilities, our study discovers a method to estimate the optimal seed size based on the target propagation size. Additionally, we found that our network design does not depend on the model used for information spread, but rather on the target propagation size. This is demonstrated through comparisons with models of controlled activation, such as the threshold model and the competing parallel transport processes.

This note addresses special Lagrangian angles, defined as Lagrangian angles that converge to zero as we move towards infinity, along with their applications and properties, especially in relation to the Chekanov model.

The effectiveness of a wireless communication system relying on a nonlinear channel model 
can be crucial to its performance during chaotic link conditions. Most communication systems 
utilize linear channel models for reliable transmissions, yet these often fail to accurately 
represent the transmission process in situations with low signal-to-noir ratios. In this study, 
the accuracy of a discrete-time channel model is examined by comparing the statistics of received 
signals with those obtained from real unamplified wireless links. These connections occasionally 
exhibit signal amplitudes exceeding a few millivolts, making traditional channel models inadequate.

Over the past few years, attack-on-encoder (AoE) attacks have been increasingly used in end-to-end neural networks for image classification, leading to significant concerns about their impact on retraining and deployment. In response to this issue, multiple instances of AoE attacks have been proposed, along with counter-measures such as regular retraining, defense systems and hardware attacks. However, a complete understanding and categorization of AoE attacks remains lacking, with no unified taxonomy to describe and differentiate them. As a result, it is difficult to identify, mitigate and develop effective defenses against these attacks. In this research, we present a new taxonomy of problem-space evasion attacks that considers the intent behind the attack launch, the method used to create malicious examples and the area of evasion within the classification model. Based on this taxonomy, we categorize and compare 15 distinct AoE attacks in terms of their intent, creation approach and location of evasion. Our analysis also discusses the open challenges and the future direction of AoE attacks and their counter-measures.

A key characteristic of modern software systems is the ability to consist of multiple services that operate independently, securely, and efficiently. Existing service orchestration typically occurs within a single container, necessitating the use of a specific runtime and management tools. This can make services difficult to deploy, manage, and move between environments. Our solution, Ozy, addresses these limitations by embedding a service container within a larger orchestration container that includes necessary runtime components and management utilities. By utilizing standard containerization technologies, Ozy enables smooth deployment, management, and portability across a wide range of execution environments. Our Ozy container is particularly small and efficient, standing at just 12MB, and has been designed with a high degree of customization and modularity in mind.

Recent studies on a fractional quantum Hall system with $n_{3D}= rac{1}{2}$ suggest the emergence of two reentrant "quantized" phases, distinct from the previously known Pfaffian ($
u=1/3$) and anti-Pfaffian ($
u=5/2$) reentrants. A new phase, previously unexamined, has been discovered at $
u=1/3$, and our calculations indicate that this phase also exists at $
u=5/2$. The distinguishing characteristic of these two new phases lies in their distinct behavior under time-reversal symmetry. Theoretical frameworks developed for the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian reentrances can be utilized to analyze the newly discovered reentrant phases.

Research into primordial black holes remains focused on their potential role in dark matter, and there's ongoing debate about constraints that can rule out their existence. Recent studies using the Thakurta metric have shown that black holes created from seismic fluctuations in the cosmic background can outperform those predicted by standard metrics, and are better equipped to dominate the dark matter market. As a result, constraints based on the Thakurrt metric are more stringent than those derived from standard metrics, and can be leveraged to rule out a broader range of primordial black holes. Furthermore, by considering how quickly density fluctuations change with scale, the Thakurta metric can place more stringent limits on certain inflationary models, and can even rule out a previously allowed range of black holes in the inflationary model known as Q-Bounce.

The process of core growth through collisions within gravitationally bound ring structures remains unclear, with no observed evidence of the predicted gravitational scattering that's thought to enhance the growth rate. Instead, we find that core growth is hindered by the same ring confinement that's necessary for it to occur in the first place. As a result, we no longer need to rely on the previously necessary assumption of significant dust injection into the system to achieve steady-state. We've also found that it's possible for the core to grow at a similar rate whether or not there's significant dust injection into the system. We've included sample calculations in appendices for specific discs in order to better understand their evolution.

Real-world applications often involve predictive models, which can function effectively without additional assumptions. In contrast, theoretical analyses often rely on extra assumptions due to an inherent information gap. This gap arises because robust learning approaches typically require fewer model parameters than non-robust methods, which means that robust learning cannot always be obtained from non-robust versions by removing or restricting assumptions to achieve similar settings. To bridge this information gap, based on a fundamental principle that all learning processes should be equivalent in terms of theoretical analysis, a new framework is proposed. This framework reinterprets and recasts a range of well-known theorems to provide robust analytical methods for a suite of machine learning algorithms, filling a significant knowledge gap in the field of adversarial robustness.

Let G be a countable abelian group denoted by the direct sum of cyclic groups of finite orders. We consider subsets $A_i$ of G for i from 1 to infinity and investigate existence/ non-existence of Bohr sets of the form $\{x\in G:|\sum_{i=1}^k x_i-\delta|<\varepsilon\}$ for given integers k, $\varepsilon$, and natural numbers $x_i$, where $\delta$ ranges over a finitely dense subgroup of G. This investigation shows that the presence/absence of such Bohr sets depends on the upper Banach density of the sumsets $A_1+\cdots+A_k$ with an exception for $k=2$, where the presence/absence depends on the Banach density of $A_1+ A_2$. Additionally, we provide examples to demonstrate that the Banach density of Bohr sets can be significantly larger than the upper Banach density of the original subsets $A_i$.

A common approach to evaluate and improve transportation solutions is to employ a simulator. The current method runs the simulation, calculate relevant metrics and feedback, and applies these to solve a constrained optimization problem. However, due to limited communication between the simulator and the optimizer, this approach only uses general traffic metrics as objectives. A more efficient strategy can be developed by leveraging specific simulation paths to tackle the original optimization problem more effectively. By integrating the simulator and optimizer closer, we can ensure that relevant information from the simulation is used to inform path adjustments. By doing so, we can reduce the total simulation time and achieve better solutions. Although this is a difficult problem from a combinatorial optimization perspective, we can employ a cut generation approach to solve it efficiently. The proposed method is tested using the Sumo traffic simulator and demonstrates significant improvements over traditional methods. Specifically, we can reduce the average simulation time by 35% while achieving a 10% better outcome.

To advance multi-modal learning, it's crucial to understand how knowledge from various sources can be effectively utilized. Typically, robust multi-modal systems are achieved by integrating multiple knowledge representations. However, a new approach proposes leveraging knowledge modalities as if they were available during training only at specific'moments of truth'. To address this limitation, Simultaneous Multi-Modal Learning can be employed by leveraging pre-trained models, enabling learning to occur concurrently with the data processing, thereby bypassing the need for intermediate training steps. A study demonstrates that this approach can lead to superior performance and higher robustness on multiple benchmark datasets, specifically ResNet-50 and ResNet-152, using transfer learning with pre-trained models on the ResNet family.

A novel approach to unsupervised learning for classification is presented, focusing on identifying similar patterns over time within individual patient data. This method detects and tracks underlying patterns, then uses them as features for classification. Notably, the approach can function without temporal information, yet incorporates temporal relationships. Its effectiveness is demonstrated by achieving comparable accuracy to supervised convolutional neural networks on classification tasks related to Alzheimer's disease progression and the detection of MCI conversion. Additionally, the approach enables meaningful, visually interpretable dimensions to be identified, which are closely aligned with established clinical metrics for monitoring disease progression.

The Backward Dropping algorithm is an unsupervised clustering method for automated word clustering based on a given text. It works by iteratively reducing word occurrences from the end of sentences, leading to the identification of words that appear together infrequently and long-term dependencies. The approach, similar to previous methods, relies on second-order bigram statistics, but unlike other clustering methods, the algorithm utilizes a sequential reduction process to identify clusters, differing from hierarchical and partition-based methods. The algorithm's performance was tested on 12 datasets from the Roman Dataset Collection and compared with six state-of-the-art methods, resulting in its current implementation achieving state-of-the-art results on 9 out of 12 datasets.

To analyze the interplay between spin-orbit interaction and electronic properties, we develop a theoretical approach to calculate the inverse life time of spin-fluctuations in strongly correlated systems. Our method, based on the extended Hubbard model, allows us to evaluate the spin-orbit interaction in terms of the two-particle correlation function. By applying this approach to the expanded Hubbard model, we investigate how spin-orbit interaction affects the electronic properties quantified by the Fermi-level spectral weight and the quasiparticle weight. Our results demonstrate that spin-orbit interaction delays the Mott transition and increases the critical point in a strongly correlated system. Furthermore, we found that spin-orbit interaction in a doped system increases with carrier doping, while it reaches a maximum in an undoped system situated on the edge of the Mott transition.

In scenarios where dark matter interacts with the Higgs field, the initial abundance of dark matter is dictated by the square of the Higgs field's vacuum expectation value, which was present in the early Universe. This implies that dark matter can be overproduced unless the Higgs field's vacuum expectation value is diminished by other processes. This problem can be mitigated if the Higgs field's vacuum expectation value is dynamically determined by other parameters, such as a scale $\Lambda$, and simultaneously reduced, leading to a viable creation of dark matter. This basic framework is applied to scenarios where dark matter is an $SU(5)$ singlet and a fermion, or a scalar, to examine how the initial abundance of dark matter is influenced by the ratio $\lambda/\Lambda^2$. This analysis demonstrates that with sufficiently small values of $\lambda/\Lambda^2$, the initial abundance of dark matter can be regulated without violating constraints on the Higgs and dark matter sectors, providing a means to explore the Higgs-dark matter sector with greater freedom. This basic framework can be expanded to incorporate additional elements, such as the active neutrinos' mass, which can act as a resonance factor, influencing the initial abundance of dark matter without breaching the active neutrinos' mass constraints. This basic framework can be adapted to accommodate various dark matter candidates, including those proposed in other theoretical frameworks, such as the Fuzzy Dark Matter model, to create a range of theoretical frameworks that can be used to forecast the

Validating the performance of uninterpretable machine learning models is a major challenge in medical image analysis. Our approach utilizes conformal prediction to enable users to make informed decisions about relevant predictions while simultaneously evaluating the model's reliability. We have developed a general method for creating conformal prediction tools applicable to black-box models in the context of classification. Our proposed procedure involves an initial training step with the black-box model and an ensemble of predictions, as well as an algorithm for generating confidence intervals and prediction intervals. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated using a medical image analysis application, where we apply ensemble methods and support vector machines to create prediction intervals for the pixel values of medical images. Our results show that the accuracy of the predictions is generally higher than without ensemble methods and that the prediction intervals successfully account for uncertainty. Additionally, the proposed tools facilitate training model comparisons and allow for a level of uncertainty quantification not previously available.

The RBB-NA algorithm offers a more efficient and accurate alternative to traditional methods for studying DNA and RNA structures. RBB-NA utilizes a model that accounts for the energy based on specific base pair interactions, reducing the complexity of the optimization process. As a result, it is well-suited for analyzing non-standard nucleic acid structures, such as those containing modified bases or intercalating agents. With RBB-NA, researchers can explore a broader range of systems, including artificial nanodevices and complex systems where structural optimization can be challenging using conventional methods. RBB-NA enables researchers to validate the structural feasibility of hypothetical systems or examine the effects of ligands on nucleic acid structure and dynamics.

This paper presents an improved variant of range-adaptive ANS (rANS) encoding, referred to as rANS with fixed accuracy (rANS-F). rANS-F addresses two primary issues associated with original rANS, including division by zero and non-constant encoding efficiency. To mitigate these problems, rANS-F involves dividing the input bitstream into fixed-size blocks, applying a parameterized compression to each block, and encoding the compressed data using a fixed accuracy, specifically 128 bits in this implementation. Experimental results demonstrate that rANS-F achieves an average encoding speed of 1.58 bytes per symbol, marking a 45% increase over rANS, with the difference largely attributed to the avoidance of division by zero in rANS-F. Furthermore, rANS-F exhibits a constant encoding efficiency and superior rate-distortion performance compared to rANS, especially at low bitrates, and its performance is comparable to that of arANS with 128 bits, the highest accuracy setting, when the input bitstream is losslessly compressed.

Concrete's dielectric characteristics can be a vital indicator of the state and durability of structures made from this material. To effectively model and analyze these properties computationally, highly accurate and detailed dielectric models are required. This research focuses on using terahertz spectroscopy to non-destructively determine the dielectric properties of concrete in its moist natural state without the need for chemical treatment. By applying the Lorentz model, we develop a precise empirical model that accurately captures the dielectric behavior of concrete with various moisture levels. Additionally, we compare the model with a theoretical model derived from fundamental frequency-dependent equations and observe a close correlation between the two. This study demonstrates the potential of the Lorentz model for use in monitoring the condition of concrete structures non-destructively.

The existence of molecular di-baryons has been well established through experiments.  In contrast, the existence of hadronic molecules composed of two heavy quarks, which are theoretically predicted to be stable since their formation is energetically favored over quark-antiquark states, has long been considered plausible.  Despite this, heavy-heavy hadronic molecules as bound states have yet to be extensively discussed in the literature.  In this study, we systematically explore the properties of various types of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules as bound states and highlight their distinct characteristics compared to di-baryotic molecules.  To this end, we examine the diquark-diquark potential model and then consider a more comprehensive quark model to obtain mass spectra and transition form factors for predicted molecular bound states, which can potentially be identified experimentally through future research.

The widespread adoption of unmanned drones has led to a surge in their availability, with the United States and Israel at the forefront of developing military drones and swarms, and China and U.S.A leading in civilian drone adoption, and Brazil leading in drone-based surveillance, as per recent studies.  In the realm of cybersecurity, a notable increase in cyberattacks has been observed, and by conducting a survey among military personnel who have experienced a change in leadership over the past 10 years, it was discovered that most common attacks are on personal devices, and U.S.A and China have seen the most cyberattacks on drones, and U.S.A and Brazil have seen the most cyberattacks on swarms.  However, it was observed that no country has been affected by cyberattacks on swarms of drones in the recent past, suggesting an underexplored area of research in this field.

A new method is developed to determine the growth term, $f\sigma_8$, and matter power spectrum, $\sigma_2$, of the non-linear matter density field from a single galaxy catalog. This is achieved through an algorithm that integrates Gaussian random fields, $N(m)$, derived from spectroscopic or weak lensing data, using a precomputed three-dimensional density field, $\delta(s)$. This approach enables accurate reconstruction of the matter density field, $\delta(s)$, to within 10% for volumes larger than 0.1 cubic gigaparsecs and provides an accurate $f\sigma_8$ measurement and $\sigma_2$ estimate. Our results show that $f\sigma_8$ can be accurately measured to within 10% at redshift $z_{ef}=2.3$ using a sufficiently large volume, and the same applies to $\sigma_2$. However, we also find that the $f\sigma_8$ measurement may be biased by the intrinsic scatter in the two-point correlation function, especially at high masses. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a biased or scattered estimate of the three-dimensional density field, $\delta(s)$, results in a significantly biased $f\sigma_8$ measurement. An innovative approach to link a low-energy beam transport line at low beam currents utilizes a TM110 single-cell cavity to introduce an electrodynamic element. This cavity is specifically designed to manipulate the particle beam's phase space and provide a clear signature in the beam dynamics for adjustment and correction purposes. A single-cell cavity has several advantages over multi-cell structures: it is lighter in design, generates a purely sinusoidal field, and is simpler in construction. A new cavity has been installed in the InfraStream low-energy beam transport line at TRIUMF and its performance has been evaluated as part of the InfraStream research activities. This study details the results from this new cavity, referred to as the QSC-1, and its impact on the beam dynamics at TRIUMF.

Predicting human pedestrian trajectories in real-world scenarios has gained significant importance, driven by the proliferation of automated driving systems and surveillance technologies. However, existing research faces limitations in their generalizability to diverse test datasets due to a phenomenon called trajectory shape bias. This bias causes prediction models to favor trajectories resembling those in the data they were trained on, resulting in lower accuracy when testing on datasets with distinct trajectory patterns. In response, we propose Shape-biased PEdestrian TRAjectory prediction method, named SPED, aimed at mitigating the impact of shape bias and enhancing cross-dataset robustness. SPED comprises two primary components: 1) a Meta-Scale network that unifies various trajectory features regardless of their shape; 2) a Shape-embedder that quantifies and reduces the influence of shape bias through an attention mechanism. SPED is evaluated using multiple public trajectory datasets and demonstrates exceptional performance in predicting paths for diverse individuals, surpassing state-of-the-art benchmarks by a considerable margin.

A key aspect of self-organization in autonomous systems is the emergence of intricate patterns of activity within the network. To investigate this concept in dynamic Boltzmann machines, we employ the technique of direct detection to analyze changes in pattern complexity over various conditions, utilizing the Detroit metric to quantify this complexity. Our results show that the Boltzmann machine's ability to organize itself and express dynamic behaviors depends on the interaction between its internal dynamics and the external flow of information. Moreover, the pattern complexity of activity patterns in the network varies directly with the network dynamics and the differences in parameters used. These findings are verified through simulations and offer a new approach to studying dynamic systems' organization and pattern formation.

A swarm of robots working together to gather data within a defined area, or coverage zone, is a key application where optimal path planning is crucial. By adjusting the distance between individual robots, a subset of the robots can exit the coverage zone, allowing others to adapt their paths and avoid collisions. To optimize this process, we've developed a math-based solution that identifies the most efficient robot reduction over time, which has been formally proven and verified through testing with a drone swarm.

anatomy into specific regions of interest and extracting relevant information
from each area. Although deep learning-based methods have excelled in region of
interest segmentation tasks, they often overlook anatomical relationships and
fail to utilize prior knowledge when generating segmentation masks. As a result,
these masks may contain inaccuracies and require modification for further

A variational approach approximates the adiabatic gauge potential, which fails to be well-defined in systems with nested regular singularities. This paper focused on computationally tractable variational approximations for the gauge potential, considering a scenario modeled by a 2x2 matrix, for which the exact renormalization technique yields variational parameters optimized according to a mathematical formula involving nested commutators. It shows that the optimal variational parameters, when expressed as squared Frobenius norms of these commutators, provide a precise estimate of the error in the approximate triangle equation known as the "magic formula." This paper, which extends to higher dimensions, offers a valuable diagnostic tool to determine the quality of the approximation and identify when the approximations, up to certain order, are insufficient. It also reveals that the nature of the singularity, for the model under consideration, determines the order of the approximations required for the "magic formula" to hold.

A widespread visual illusion is the perception of warm colors being red and the perception of cool colors being blue. This effect is achieved through the use of chromatic aberration, a phenomenon where red light is separated from other colors as it passes through a lens. We propose a method to simulate this effect using digital images by selectively shifting the red channel pixels by varying amounts. To achieve a natural appearance, the amount of shift is determined based on the pixel's distance from the image center and its intensity. The effect can be observed by viewing the red channel using a color picker or through a red filter.

This research provides a background on the growth of the $C^r$ class and establishes conditions under which infinite series and integrals converge, including a newly discovered integral of convergent $C^{r+m}$ functions that was previously unknown. Furthermore, it formulates two problems related to the growth of the $C^r$ class and provides significant evidence in support of one of the hypotheses.

A closed surface $M$ with a metric $g$ possessing an upper curvature bound is conferred with the $CD(k)$ structure. We prove in this study that if a conformally equivalent pair of surfaces $(M, g)$ and $(M, h)$ satisfy the $CD(0)$ condition and their conformal factor $\rho$ realises the conformal distortion minimally, then these surfaces are geometrically distinct yet conformally equivalent to one another. This generalises Chen's and Hong's previous findings. Under the assumption that $M$ equates to the 2-sphere $S^2$ conformally equivalent to the hyperbolic 2-sphere, we present several optimal criteria.

Researchers have made significant progress in recent years in the field of laser-wakefield acceleration, which now shows promise for high-energy physics research. A novel concept called an "electron photon source" can convert the energy of relativistic electrons into high-energy photon beams, specifically in the MeV to GeV range. Such a source, powered by a laser-wakefield accelerator, can produce these photons over a broad energy spectrum, offering a more efficient alternative to traditional Bremsstrahlung sources. Additionally, this electron photon source can create hard X-ray pulses by exploiting the betatron radiation of intense electron beams within plasma-filled waveguides. These pre-ionized plasma regions can produce a rich spectrum of soft and hard X-rays. Moreover, the radiation emitted by plasma oscillations or the lasing itself can further fill out this photon spectrum. Presently, the development of an "electron photon source" remains a topic of exploration, but it has the potential to significantly expand the capabilities of existing electron accelerators and open up new opportunities for research in high-energy photon experiments.

This has yielded new insights into Higgs-fermion-fermion vertex form factors, allowing for precise measurements of Higgs boson decays.
