We revisit and revise the universal solutions for data exchange, particularly focusing on key-covered situations where a global key exists for a instance of a relational schema. Initially, this concept was defined by Schwindln and Kracht but yielded an instance with no universal solution and an ambiguous existence for others. Our work refines the definition, ensuring a universal solution exists and clarifies the existence of others. Additionally, we extend the definition to key-set-covered situations, where a collection of global keys is present for a data instance.

We introduce pyStoNED, a newly developed Python package that facilitates
interfacing with Gnu Octave's StoNED framework. StoNED utilizes vectorized
operations and object-oriented overloading to enhance the efficiency of
multivariate regression and machine learning algorithms. pyStNED enables seamless
transitions between Python and Gnu Octave, allowing users to leverage the
strengths of both environments. We provide detailed instructions and showcase
pyStNED's capabilities by performing non-linear least squares optimization and
generating synthetic data sets. Additionally, we compare pyStNED with other
Python libraries through numerical simulations.

The High Luminosity phase of the Large Hadron Collider offers exceptional possibilities for analyzing the properties of light scalar particles, which are a key aspect of various theories extending the Standard Model. This study compares the potential of two major detection systems, the CMS detector in conjunction with the SHARK and HL-LHC detectors, all of which are capable of efficiently identifying light scalar particles using the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ decay process. By examining two types of events resulting from the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ decay, the research calculates the optimal sensitivity for detecting Yukawa couplings for particles with masses less than 30 GeV. Notably, the analysis yields exclusion limits at the 10^3 sigma level for CP-even and CP-odd Yukawa couplings for particles with masses close to 10 GeV. This achievement surpasses the current benchmark limits set by the ATLAS and CMS Collaborations by nearly one order of magnitude. Moreover, the research demonstrates that the SHARK detector offers improved sensitivity compared to the HL-LHC detector for particles with predominantly CP-odd properties.

We introduce FPIO, an innovative few-shot parsing model that achieves exceptional performance with minimal training examples. With a unique combination of an encoder, decoder, and copy mechanism, FPIO adapts to novel languages without requiring retraining, significantly outperforming previous models by at least 5 F-Score points with less than 10 examples per sentence. FPIO's capabilities are showcased on eight diverse languages, including three under-resourced languages, and its source code and model are freely available online for further exploration.

This study investigates how diverse training data enhances the speech recognition model's speaker adaptation and topic shift resilience. A large dataset with numerous public resources is utilized, and its impact on the model's robustness is evaluated using different diversity metrics, such as relative entropy and domain coverage. Experimental results indicate that incorporating data from various domains leads to enhanced generalizability, and higher domain coverage and relative entropy in training data result in better speaker adaptation and topic shift robustness. Notably, the study finds that a model trained on data with moderate diversity, as measured by domain coverage of approximately 0.20, outperforms one trained with data that has low diversity or data that is highly redundant. These findings provide valuable insights for selecting training data effectively and optimizing the performance of speech recognition models in new contexts.

Using data from the SONG nodes at S\'OAR and G\'ENOVA, the observation and data analysis techniques employed to study binary systems in the context of the SONG network were tested and validated. This involved measuring the binary frequencies of Be and normal Be stars, which yielded 13 binary systems out of 74 observed Be stars, resulting in a binary frequency of approximately 18%. In contrast, only 5 binary systems were found out of 46 normal B-type stars, corresponding to a binary frequency of about 11%. These results are consistent with existing literature and reveal a notable difference in binary frequencies between Be and normal Be stars, which is also consistent with existing literature and reveals a notable difference in binary frequencies between Be and normal B-type stars. Furthermore, the observed and derived properties and characteristics of these binary systems show good agreement between spectroscopic and photometric data.

This study presents a novel data augmentation approach, utilizing a pre-trained language model to generate guide sentences for in-domain and out-of-domain text data. The guide sentence is employed as a prompt, which initiates a conditional text generation process to produce augmented text. Evaluations conducted on three information extraction tasks demonstrate the proposed method's capability to achieve in-domain and out-of-domain training with a single model, surpassing performance compared to conventional training methods. Additionally, this approach's effectiveness is further verified by training models under various parameter configurations, encompassing distinct network architectures, input representations, and learning objectives.

The study focuses on the spectral properties of compact non-compact selfadjoint operators on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a singular compact perturbation corresponding to the Hermite operator. A Faber-Krahn type inequality is demonstrated for the first eigenvalue, showing that an optimal configuration occurs when the boundaries meet at a right angle. Additionally, the work investigates the spectral behavior in the case of a Gaussian distribution and a Robin boundary condition with a positive parameter. In this scenario, the spectral function behaves as $N(\lambda)$ and the spectral asymptotics are examined, revealing that $N(\lambda)$ grows logarithmically with $\lambda$.

Deep neural networks possess exceptional performance on various challenging tasks but their complex nature hinders their internal workings and generalizability. Research has discovered that neural tangent kernels (NTKs), both with and without the use of traditional deep networks, exhibit more predictable behavior and enhanced generalizability. This study compares the predictive capabilities of NTKs, neural networks, and random feature models on specific datasets (binomial and Gaussian) by examining their behavior in the limit of an infinitely large number of features. By analyzing models trained with a variety of methods, including a novel approach utilizing a mean-field approximation, we find that NTKs, when paired with tangent feature kernels, display consistent predictive capabilities across different training methods. In contrast, neural networks demonstrate a smoother loss landscape compared to NTKs, which in turn explains the improved performance of neural networks on certain tasks after further training based on their structural differences.

The impact of finite-size effects and edge effects needs to be carefully considered in non-Hermitian systems, especially in the context of the Hatano-Nelson chain when extended to include nearest-neighbor hopping. By analyzing the eigenvalue statistics and the survival probability of this extended Hatano-Nelson chain, it has been observed that correlations among weakly bounded states lead to a non-uniform distribution of eigenvalues at long distances, resulting in a skin effect. The extended Hatano-Nelson chain exhibits a skin effect that is distinct from that of the original model and an analogous random matrix model. Additionally, it has been found that a non-Hermitian quantum system's wave function localization can be influenced by correlations among weakly bounded states.

Previous research has shown that averaging speech profiles from different speakers can go undetected by listeners, suggesting a potential for synthesized speech that's indistinguishable from human. Yet, speech technology often prioritizing realism over uniqueness. The aim of this study is to explore whether combining profiles can also impact the credibility of the synthesized speech. We manipulated the speech profiles of a female synthesizer to represent either high or low authority figures and found that listeners perceived the synthesized speech as authoritative. Furthermore, listeners preferred the profile that matched their task goal - either high or low authority. When given a choice, listeners tended to prefer the profile that aligned with their goal. These results suggest that manipulating speech profiles can not only make the speech more believable, but also convey specific characteristics such as authority.

We present a modified version of the Yukawa Dark Matter model that remains stable with a long lifespan and addresses the issues of dark matter and neutrino mass. The model's simplicity and stability are attributed to a $U(1)_{X_1} \times U(1)_{X_2}$ symmetry, where the symmetry generator, $X_1$, annihilates the dark matter when it is not in a bound state with a neutrino, preventing overabundance. The other symmetry generator, $X_2$, is responsible for stabilizing dark matter as it prevents the decay of the dark sector into standard particles. The model requires the introduction of a second heavy scalar, $\phi'$, in addition to the Higgs field, to generate the dark matter mass and facilitate the resonant annihilation of dark matter. The model's parameters are constrained by several conditions including the relic density, the upper limit on neutrino mass, and the upper limit on dark matter mass. The model's parameters are also constrained by requiring a successful freeze-in production of dark matter. The results show that the model's parameters are tightly constrained with a lower bound on the mass of the scalar, $m_\phi$, and a lower bound on the coupling between dark matter and the scalar, $g_{DM, \phi}$.

This research investigates how the effects of space shortening on triaxial nuclei's energy levels relate to their angular momentum. To achieve this, we developed a modified version of the Wigner-Dymnikov Hamiltonian that incorporates the effects of minimal length parameter (m) into a real quadratic deformed eigenvalue problem. The resulting Hamiltonian is then applied to a specific type of nucleus with 6 degrees of freedom, and the resulting eigenvalues are found to be well-described by a modified semiempirical mass formula. The impact of varying the minimal length parameter on these eigenvalues is explored, and the relationship between nuclear structure and the minimal length parameter is discussed. Our findings suggest that the effects of minimal length parameter (m) could potentially be used to distinguish specific aspects of nuclear structure.

We provide a complete description of the quaternary Golay complementary array (GCA) 
feasibility condition, then analyze the properties of feasible GCAs of lengths 
$2^n-1$, where $n$ must be either 3, an even prime, a power of 2 times a prime, 
or a product of two odd primes. We present all possible quaternary GCAs of lengths 
$2^n-1$ for the given cases of $n$.

Change detection in urban environments is essential for monitoring and planning. Unsupervised change detection methods can be effective without needing extensive labeled data. However, their performance may be limited when compared to supervised methods. In this study, changes in Istanbul's landscape between 2004 and 2014 were identified using supervised and unsupervised change detection techniques. Unsupervised change detection, based on random forest clustering, revealed various clusters with hidden changes. By manually filtering these clusters, many accurate changes were found. Although some accurate changes were missed, others were mistakenly classified as false positives. Compared to supervised change detection, unsupervised method required less data filtering and less time. Nonetheless, supervised change detection was more efficient overall.

The schedule for updating the density scaling and viscosity mapping for the ReaxFF atomistic force field is being reviewed. The evaluation focuses on non-associating molecular fluids and how the flexibility of molecular bonds influences the accuracy of viscosity predictions. The study found that by using the same functional form as before, but with updated parameters, the density scaling does not introduce errors when applied to different molecular size groups, similar to how the original parameter set behaves. The new parameter set also maintains chemical compatibility while maintaining equivalent viscosity mappings across various molecular size groups. The error analysis showed that the density scaling approach reduces average errors to less than 5% for both size-reduced and expanded simulations, demonstrating its high level of transferability. The original parameter set was also evaluated for size transferability and was found to have similar performance as the new one, but with larger errors to predict viscosities of fluids with significantly different molecular size. The review concludes by recommending the density scaling and viscosity mapping approach for use with the ReaxFF atomistic force field, particularly for modeling and simulating non-associating molecular fluids.

A new model of cosmology is suggested, which is called the periodic cosmology model. This model effectively combines elements from the inflationary theory and theories of expansion acceleration, representing a self-similar relationship between these concepts. In the model, there are two separate phases - a Lambda CDM phase that occurs at small scales and an inflationary phase that occurs at large scales. Interestingly, during the transition between these phases, a brief period of contracting expansion is observed. Various aspects of the model, including its ability to match observations of cosmic microwave background radiation, are explored in detail.

The concept of measuring a quantum state without disturbing it raises questions about the need for entanglement due to two related ideas - counterfactual measurements and measurement independence. These concepts are often discussed under the umbrella of nonlocality but actually demonstrate fundamental local aspects of quantum theory, resolving debates by allowing the use of independent measurements that are also counterfactual. Measurements that don't affect each other are also counterfactual without entanglement and vice versa, and we show how local realisms can explain nonlocal phenomena, illustrating this with the Bell test and quantum teleportation. These concepts highlight fundamental local aspects of quantum theory that simplify and clarify nonlocal phenomena.

Neural networks, crucial to numerous AI applications, continually evolve and improve in their design variants.  Their implementation on devices such as smart speakers and wearable devices remains challenging due to their large size in memory and the computational resources they require.  To improve usage lifetimes and reduce power consumption, it is essential to explore ways to lower the overhead of neural network implementation.  To this end, we have compiled a comprehensive dataset of various neural network models and their estimated computational needs.  Our dataset, known as "MemNet", includes detailed specifications for over 65 million model configurations, enabling researchers and engineers to quickly assess the memory and processing requirements of multiple neural network models.  By utilizing this dataset, we are able to analyze trends in the complexity of different models and the impact of parameter optimization techniques.  Furthermore, we have validated the accuracy of certain memory estimation methods and the advantages of reducing a model's dimensionality to lower the overall overhead of neural network implementation.

A novel expansion of the dimer model on isorial graphs is developed, leveraging a refined cluster expansion technique that preserves term-by-term equivalence.  This analysis yields a concise formula for the dimer model's cluster expansion, however the generated series is subject to a significant shift in its first term.  By applying a specific cluster truncation, the exact partition function can be computed, yet this approach incurs an O(n^(1/2)) error rate.  By contrast, removing the first term and performing cluster truncation yields a series that converges rapidly to the partition function, specifically at a rate of O(n^(-3/2 + ε) for any ε > 0).  By matching the dimer model's cluster expansion with the holomorphic gauged worm function, the exact partition function can be precisely computed, thus confirming prior results.  By contrast, the holomorphic gauging method itself is subject to a relatively slow O(n^(-1/2 + ε) convergence rate for any ε > 0).

We've developed a new algorithm for multivariate response regression analysis that performs variable selection in cases involving continuous or categorical data. Our proposed Group Lasso method introduces penalties based on the Fiedler norm, enabling the selection of groups of variables as single units. The algorithm's consistency and convergence rates have been established under general conditions, and its reliability demonstrated through applications to synthetic and real-world data sets, including genomic expression analysis and cancer treatment outcome prediction in high-dimensional studies. A standalone implementation of the algorithm can be accessed at https://github.com/JuliaDiscreteOptimization/GroupLasso.

T-Visor is a lightweight hypervisor developed for embedded systems with diverse real-time requirements. By nature, a hypervisor affects the scheduling of Guest-OSes it runs, but T-Visor's flexible design accommodates various scheduling needs within its framework. In this study, we demonstrate how T-Visor's scheduling functionality works and propose a universal scheduling model. This model serves as a general guideline for applications using multiple Guest-OSes and addresses their real-time needs. We present a universal scheduling algorithm based on the proposed model and conduct experiments to illustrate its efficiency and effectiveness. These experiments cover different preemption levels, Guest-OS contexts, and Visitor thread scheduling. We also compare T-Visor's performance to hard real-time executives (HRTEs) in terms of context switching and Visitor thread scheduling. In a real-world application, we apply the Visitor thread scheduling concept to improve the responsiveness of graphical user interfaces in embedded systems.

A novel approach to creating panoramic images without external support is presented, leveraging the accuracy of Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) to compensate for the limitations of camera capture resolution. A specific device configuration - comprising an IMU and a wide-angle camera - allows for accurate angular calculation, enabling the creation of high-resolution panoramic images. A novel algorithm, designed for use with a single rotation, synthesizes images captured at close angles and accounts for distortion caused by rotation. By combining IMU data and camera capture synchronization, this method can produce high-resolution panoramic images. A specific algorithm implementation called Swirl is introduced, along with a new hardware configuration that maximizes image quality. Experiments confirm that Swirl outperforms existing panoramic capture methods, with notable improvements in image resolution and overall performance.

Research on chimeric states in complex networks is currently limited, particularly for networks consisting of multiple groups of oscillators. In this study, we use a simplified model to investigate the chimeric states that arise in networks of three oscillators within different groups, where the within-group connections follow a specified rule and the between-group connections are variable. By adjusting the strength of these variable connections, we identified chimeric states that exhibit instability upon further changes in this strength. Interestingly, increasing the diversity among oscillators in these groups can lead to the stabilization of these chimeric states. Additionally, we found that the phase differences within and between chimeric states are not fixed, but rather exhibit a range of values, which can even change over time in non-repeating patterns. These findings provide valuable groundwork for further research on chimeric states in more complex networks.

Numerous studies demonstrate that learning a dynamical system's equation from observed data leads to robust control strategies, however, they typically lack an underlying guarantee for the accuracy of the learned model itself. In this research, we address this issue by introducing a constraint that ensures a lower bound for the likelihood noise level in the dynamics model, effectively limiting the prediction error. By incorporating this constraint into an existing optimization framework for nonlinear control systems, we provide formal assurances for the accuracy of the learned model and the safety of the learned controller. Furthermore, we show that enforcing this bound leads to a controller with increased resistance to failure. We also present practical methods for approximating the constraint, reducing to approach real-world problems. The proposed approach is demonstrated using a quadrotor dynamics model learned from video and a 3D simulation environment, where the learned model's increase in robustness is verified.

The matrix and tensor algebras for a quiver $Q$ have natural connections to the construction of a quiver's slice algebra $R=\mathbb{K}\Gamma(Q,k)$, where $\Gamma$ represents a specific algebraic structure and $k$ is a nonnegative integer. By examining the relationship between these algebras and their connections to strata in the slice algebra, we can determine combinatorial descriptions for particular types of structures within $R$. By applying this approach to various types of quivers, it allows for the identification of specific elements within $R$, including combinatorial descriptions for characters in types $A$ and $B$, and relations to other areas of study, such as the Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality and the Littlewood-Richardson rule.

Real-world applications of quantum entanglement spectra, particularly those involving random networks, have led to novel uses of the R'enyi entanglement spectrum. We have found that certain applications of the R'enyi spectrum are limited due to their inability to distinguish non-trivial bipartite substructures. To address this limitation, we have developed a reflected R'enyi spectrum, a modification of the standard R'enyi spectrum, which can detect these differences. Unlike standard R'enyi spectra, the reflected versions are sensitive to the structure of random tensor networks, even those generated by random matrix ensembles. We have demonstrated this with a family of examples, including a specific instance of a random tensor network previously believed to exhibit a non-trivial entanglement spectrum according to the usual R'enyi spectra analysis. In contrast, the reflected spectra reveal that this example in fact exhibits a trivial entanglement spectrum. We have further shown that the reflected spectra can distinguish between weakly entangled and non-entangled bipartitions.

The concept of probability of persistence for large sets of dynamical systems has been explored, with the findings that even random small changes can result in significant probabilistic outcomes when observing persistent dynamics over extended periods.  We have established that this probability is influenced by the distance between the system's target set and its surrounding sets, with specific metrics that have been shown to be nonincreasing under various system transformations.  Notably, this probability cannot be bounded below by an analogous measure, highlighting its sensitivity to the system's structure.  Our research demonstrates the application of these results to diverse systems, such as random dynamical systems, linear systems subject to stochastic disturbances, and nonlinear systems characterized by discontinuous dynamics.  In particular, this study reveals the connection between the system's probability of persistence and the properties of random walks on graphs, with the findings that even random walks with finite range can lead to infinite probabilities of reaching distant locations.

We analyze the structural elements within the parameter space of quadratic diffeomorphisms, focusing specifically on the spectral indicators of non-hyperbolic cycles. The introduction of periodic cycle orbits significantly influences the parameter space organization, necessitating a modification of the existing ordering based on linear iterations. By incorporating spectral indicators from non-hyperbolic cycles, we create an enhanced and more accurate ordering, achieving greater precision in determining the Lyapunov spectrum and stability properties for all quadratic diffeomorphisms. Additionally, we uncover previously unknown results regarding the application of H\'enon's iterates, which play a pivotal role in distinguishing unstable orbits, and reveal the importance of numerical methods in identifying non-persistence cycles via Lyapunov spectrum analysis.

This work explores geometric and dynamical characteristics of gravity holonomies.
Research reveals that gravity holonomies are contingent on the metric's underlying structure.
Notably, gravity holonomies in general are non-gauge-theory-type holonomies, except in the flat case.
A novel, self-consistent gravity theory, based on vanishing holonomies, is proposed and developed.

The classical limit theorem of Narumi and Watanabe (1978) asserts that as n approaches infinity, the distribution of (max(0, X_1^n +... + X_1^n)) approaches the distribution of |N(0,1)|. This paper generalizes this result by proving that as n approaches infinity, the distribution of (max(0, abs(X_1^n +... + X_1^n))) closely approximates the distribution of (max(0, abs(U_1^n +... + U_1^n))) where X_i and U_i are independent, zero-mean, unit-variance standard normal and uniform variables on (-1,1).

A novel formulation of the actual tunneling time has been developed using the quantum transition rate from one bound state to another, specifically from the ground state to the first excited state of a one-dimensional square well potential. This new approach utilizes spin fluctuations as the key element, in contrast to previous tunneling time methodologies. Interestingly, the new tunneling time can take on either value, potentially even exceeding the classical crossing time, and its behavior is sensitively influenced by the spin parameter of the potential. Moreover, the new time evolution parameter not only works for tunneling but also accurately describes the quantum decay process for a square well potential with spin-dependent boundary conditions.

This research investigates relativistic corrections to amplitudes containing P-wave charmonia mesons. Specifically, it examines relativistic corrections to processes involving the production of $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$, as well as certain reactions involving LHCb's detection capabilities, such as $\bar B^0_s \to J/\psi f_0(980)$, $\bar B^0_s \to \psi(2S) f_0(1370)$, and $\bar B^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0$. To achieve this, relativistic corrections are applied to factorizable amplitudes within a relativistic independent particle model. As a result, relativistic corrections to these processes are determined in both a relativistic and a non-relativistic framework, with the former demonstrating more significant impacts. With the obtained relativistic corrections validated through a comparison of factorizable and dominant non-relativistic amplitudes, this study provides a crucial foundation for further research and potential applications at LHCb.

Our research explores the precise creation of quantum states within a three-level quantum system consisting of multiple entangled atoms. By applying an optimized, yet imperfect series of laser pulses, we successfully manufacture a tripartite entangled state within a group of atoms within a specific energy range. We find that, despite the imperfections in the laser pulses, it is possible to achieve near perfect entanglement using a specific algorithm. We further demonstrate that, due to the rapid evolution of the quantum states during the process, our method achieves the highest rate of entanglement production in a given timeframe. We then show how, by utilizing this near perfect entangled state within a Ramsey interferometry system, it is possible to achieve the highest rate of entanglement production in a given timeframe. Utilizing this near perfect entangled state within a Ramsey interferometry system, we achieve the highest sensitivity possible, surpassing the standard quantum precision. We find that the rate of entanglement production in our method is most sensitive to variations in the duration of the laser pulses that affect the evolution of the quantum states. Consequently, we propose a new method of measuring the optical phase that leverages the near perfect entangled state within a Ramsey interferometry system, utilizing a fast measurement of the optical phase with high accuracy. We show that, despite the presence of imperfections in the quantum states, our method achieves a high rate of entanglement production in a given timeframe. The investigation into defining time depends heavily on a two-part approach: first, understanding the characteristics of states in classical and quantum mechanics, and second, exploring its application in three-dimensional gravity. In this study, we delve into the classical theory of state definitions, particularly focusing on a well-established framework known as BMS charges, which includes de Mello, Magueijo, and Sasaki's work on a specific type of charge. We demonstrate how certain properties of vacuums in defined states, such as degeneracies and entropy, can be attributed to "soft news" and "Schwarzian modes." We observe that, from a theoretical standpoint, these modes, which set the initial conditions for defined states, are essentially null surfaces in anti-de Sitter space. Additionally, we find that, when considering all possible null surfaces, the EFT volume, which forms the basis of a gravitational action's expansion, emerges naturally. In quantum theory, which is the focus of our subsequent study, we establish that, as with classical states, defined time is rooted in a fundamental mode known as the quantum news mode, which determines the initial conditions for quantum definitions.

Ensemble methods within deep neural network training are gaining traction, 
notably after the notable success of Deep Ensemble in winning the 2018 
Blizzard Song Identification Task. Yet, standard ensemble methods prove 
inefficient for handling RNNs due to increased memory requirements and 
computation costs. This research presents an innovative ensemble approach 
for reducing the collision issue during RNN feature extraction, enabling 
the creation of ensembles for deep RNNs. This novel technique also allows 
the application of variance reduction methods, ultimately resulting in 
lower training and testing error rates when compared to individual RNNs 
and previous ensemble methods such as bagging and bootstrapping.

The construction of generalized connections is a crucial aspect in various fields such as
supergravity and generalized complex geometry.  Our study shows that these connections
are inherently linked with Ricci flat metrics.  By establishing a relationship between
generalized geometry and a generalized supergravity framework, we demonstrate that
introducing a generalized spin connection allows for the derivation of a generalized
super gravitino projection operator.  This, in turn, facilitates the construction of
a generalized twist that connects generalized complex and generalized complex duality
without requiring the super gravitino projection operator.  Additionally, we explore
the relationship between generalized geometry and solutions to N=1* and N=2* super
gravities in four and three geometries, respectively, particularly focusing on the
special Karlsson case.

We propose a concept of complete mapping for polynomial functions over finite fields in the context of composite moduli. Building upon this idea, we develop methods to decompose composite moduli into a set of complete mappings, similar to the prime power factorization process. Next, we establish the Chinese Remainder Theorem's extended version for this specific application. Furthermore, we create two types of bilinear forms over finite fields in the context of complete mappings and explore their properties, particularly in relation to their rank, determinant, and orthogonality characteristics.

Inspection of human feces is the traditional method for identifying intestinal parasites.
Although widely used and relatively low-cost, this method is prone to inaccuracies.
Conversely, automated parasite detection through image analysis is considered the gold standard.
We propose combining human visual inspection with the power of machine learning by using
images taken during inspections in a deep learning framework to enhance detection accuracy. 
By integrating meta information about images, such as camera make and orientation, we
aim to increase the effectiveness of this method and reduce errors by accounting for variations
in image capture. This image-based system is designed to be compatible with various cameras, 
including those used by human visual inspectors, thereby facilitating the integration of human
expertise into image analysis to increase the reliability of automated systems.

This study utilizes the viscosity solution approach to resolve a set of nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, represented as a free boundary value problem. The equations can be found at https://www.math.ucla.edu/~mjlee/Annals2022.pdf. By applying the viscosity solution approach, we derive existence and uniqueness of the solution, even in the presence of irregularities in the state space. The proof relies on specific perturbation arguments and the stability of viscosity solutions when constraints change. The work builds on previous research in the field, mentioned in https://arxiv.org/ark:/44404/1111.0901.

A quadcopter's dynamic model including external influences like wind can be counteracted by integrating a counter-measure algorithm. To tackle the issue of unpredictable disturbances, a control technique grounded on the Linear Quadratic Regulator method is proposed, which involves a real-time calculation of system dynamics adaptation. The proposed method utilizes an estimation algorithm inspired by a Genetic Filter to predict the external effects and adjust the quadcopter's motion accordingly. Simulation results show the efficacy of this approach by demonstrating error minimization and stability even without the occurrence of expected disturbances. Furthermore, the algorithm's adaptability is validated through tests involving unpredictable random disturbances.

The pion-nucleon sigma term, a critical element in evaluating nuclear forces and pion-nucleon scattering data, holds significant importance. Although it can be calculated using lattice QCD with good accuracy, its dominant part is still unclear due to the lack of understanding of the light quark strangeness and the presence of corrections from charm quarks. To address this limitation, an attempt is made to derive the nucleon matrix elements of strangeness-changing operators, thereby allowing for the calculation of the proton's strangeness response function. Additionally, an investigation into the isospin-breaking effects of quark masses and electromagnetic interactions on the proton's strangeness response is conducted.

The CMS detector's silicon pixel sensor ensemble, featuring high-grading forward detectors and two-layer rear-end detectors, has been operating since 2016. Following a significant upgrade in 2017-2018, the CMS detector boasts a high level of efficiency and purity in particle selection. Nevertheless, the detector's high-rate environments and radiation during prolonged operations have presented challenges to the front-end readout chip's trigger capabilities. In response, the CMS collaboration has undertaken an extensive upgrade of the detector's readout system for the 2019-2020 data collection period. A cutting-edge, off-detector farm-based software trigger has been developed to compensate for these limitations, allowing the front-end readout chip's maximum hit count limit to be effectively doubled. A detailed description of the upgraded readout system, incorporating advanced software and hardware capabilities, is presented here.

Using the X-ray and optical bands, we have attempted to identify the host galaxies of 91 actively galactic nuclei located at X-ray fluxes ranging from $3.9\times10^{-15}$ to $6.1\times10^{-14}$ erg s$^{-1}$ (0.2-8 keV). The X-ray luminosity of these AGN, measured via our observations with the Chandra X-ray telescope, correlates well with their optical Baldwin effect and allows for an efficient selection of host galaxies based on their Baldwin effect values. The X-ray-to-optical spectral gradient ratio is used to separate AGN candidates into two groups. While 53 galaxies qualify as strong AGN hosts, our analysis reveals that the precision of AGN host galaxy classification varies depending on the redshift interval, achieving a 75% and 30% classification accuracy at $z<0.5$ and $z>1$, respectively. The X-ray and optical data prove to be complementary tools, allowing us to study the relationship between AGN and their host galaxies at varying redshifts.

The neutron skin thickness in isotopic series of lead and tin isotopes has been computed using high-resolution quantum mechanics. Calculations are based on experimental data involving scattering of aluminum and silicon ions as well as lead and lead and tin fixed nucleus experiments. Employing a novel correlation method that accurately accounts for short-range interactions in nuclear asymmetric systems, we analyzed neutron distribution in a range of isotopes. Our analysis of fixed nucleus data suggests a direct link between the neutron skin and a correlation coefficient that diminishes in intensity with increasing neutron number. Additionally, we observed that a shift in the neutron distribution towards the center occurs when the number of protons approaches the mid-point between neutron and proton number.

We introduce a novel method for representing RGB images through complex-valued scaling transformations. This allows us to analyze and interpret the effects of geometric transformations on color patterns. By associating scaling with complex factors, we can easily identify equivalent transformations, eliminate redundancy, and distinctively identify unique similarity transformations. This form of representation simplifies image registration, enabling us to align images through translation, rotation, and scaling without necessity for interpolation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques in image registration across various datasets and metrics. Moreover, it naturally facilitates tasks like object detection and tracking by allowing us to directly apply detection criteria and tracking algorithms at the original image size, without needing to downsize the image as is typically done. This new approach also provides a unified understanding of traditional RGB image representations, revealing how certain image features are created by geometric scalings. Consequently, it enables us to quantify the effects of hue shifts and color channel correlations, ultimately leading to improved image reproduction methods.

The concept of geometrical scaling in hadronic reactions is examined, involving gluon distribution saturation. Analyzing collisions between electrons and ions at HERA, as well as those between heavy nuclei, we find evidence of geometrical scaling applying over a specific range of energy density. We observe that leading order perturbation theory accurately describes the data within this range but fails to explain data at higher energy densities. Our findings suggest that geometrical scaling applies within this intermediate range due to the onset of gluon distribution saturation, which may be further understood through a simple mean field calculation. Additionally, we identify the point at highest energy density examined in our study as the boundary beyond which geometrical scaling applies.

To investigate how core-collapse supernovae (CCSN) influenced the chemical composition of the early universe, we integrated the CCSN rate into the \texttt{GALFORM} model. The unique aspects of our study include utilizing a stochastic sampling of the CCSN progenitor mass distribution and applying a metal cutoff to the CCSN rate equation. By simulating the mass of CCSN progenitors from a given distribution on a fine scale and summing the resulting metal contributions, we accounted for the diverse nature of CCSN events. The model also accounted for the effects of shell-nucleosynthesis following explosion and starlight from nearby explosions for ejected CCSEne elements. The enriched material from CCSNe affects the gas within a given halo, leading to altered star formation and element abundance predictions. The introduction of these CCSEne elements resulted in decreased predictions of [Fe/H] and predictions that fall below observed values in various studies. The unique characteristics of our model, such as stochastic sampling and metal cutoff, have the potential to resolve the issue of underproduced alpha elements observed in the early galaxy. The inclusion of CCSEne elements may improve predictions of [O/H] and [Mg/H] in certain situations but does not fully resolve the issue of underproduced oxygen. The additional production of elements from CCSNe does not significantly alter the predicted redshift of the peak cosmic infrared background intensity at 850 $\mu$m.

The concept of model stability in predictive models involves assessing how resilient the model is to the addition of synthetic predictors. A model exhibiting stability signifies that its performance remains consistent when including or excluding additional artificial variables. Notably, some models demonstrate stability regardless of the correlation between the synthetic predictors and their performance, whereas others may achieve optimal performance only when correlated with the target variable. We investigated the stability characteristics of six prominent predictive models, namely Bayesian Additive Regression Trees, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Support Vector Regression, K-nearest Neighbors, and Linear Regression, using synthetic data with varying properties through an extensive simulation study. The results indicated substantial variations in the stability of these models according to their construction, with some models being inherently stable and others not demonstrating a significant difference in performance between correlated and uncorrelated synthetic predictors.

Variational quantum models, incorporating gradient-based optimization on a classical computer to aid in training quantum models, show potential as powerful quantum simulators. Their potential largely depends on the output of the quantum circuit used. This study compares four different outputs of variational quantum models in terms of optimization efficiency: (i) a Pauli measurement on multiple qubits, (ii) a measurement on a single qubit with appropriate Pauli operators, (ii) a binary output via projective measurement, and (iv) a multi-class classification problem treated as a probability vector. Numerical experiments using a variational quantum circuit on up to 9 qubits show that output (ii) generally performs best, with output (i) showing comparable performance on smaller systems and output (iv) showing better performance on very large systems. Output (iii) proved to be the least efficient. This study emphasizes the need to carefully select the output of variational quantum models to maximize optimization efficiency.

This research delves into the properties of a particular geometric structure, pointwise semi-slant warped product submanifolds, in the context of Sasakian manifolds and certain related almost contact metric manifolds. The investigation is then focused on the more specific case of 3-dimensional warped product submanifolds. The findings indicate that no 3-dimensional semi-slant warped product submanifold exists on a Sasakian manifold. A more surprising discovery is that no 3-dimensional mixed slant warped product submanifold can be found in a Kenmotsu manifold, nor in any 3-dimensional or 4-dimensional $alpha$-Sasakian manifolds.

A groundbreaking direct neutrino detection technique utilizes advanced particle sensors to identify and count the interactions of neutrinos with atomic nuclei, particularly important for deep-underground experiments. The Majorana collaboration is currently developing a direct neutrino detector with advanced technology to identify and count the interactions of CEvNS on lead nuclei. The experiment's detailed analysis of its ongoing measurements with the MonoE voltage-mode neutron detector, a cutting-edge large-volume liquid-argon particle sensor, is presented in this study. The findings of the experiment, taking place at the Sanford Research Facility at a depth of 2,150 meters water-equivalent, with 8.9 metric tons of lead and an exposure period of 192 days in 2021, are presented. The experiment's results, demonstrating high sensitivity to various processes, are discussed in detail. The research further marks the first-ever direct neutrino detection experiment using CEvNS on lead nuclei, a significant milestone in the field of neutrino research. The findings of the experiment, in conjunction with comprehensive simulations, demonstrate the high potential of the MonoE technology to significantly improve the detection limits for various rare processes at shallow depths.

Our research demonstrates that active dimers can overcome topological barriers, with their behavior being influenced by an external steering mechanism. The external drive can be applied in a direction that's not supported by the underlying crystal structure, resulting in a deflection angle proportional to the distance from the original driving position and the crystal lattice parameter. A simplified theoretical model was developed to explain the experimental outcomes, showcasing the relationship between the area enclosed by the crystal lattice parameter and the deflection angle. Furthermore, it was found that hydrodynamic forces play a negligible role in this specific system. The experimental results presented here offer a new perspective on active matter's ability to traverse topological barriers and represent one of the most significant manifestations of its 'geometric control' capabilities.

Theoretical findings suggest the existence of magnetorotons in twisted moiré superlattices at fractional fillings. Recent experiment on a moiré bilayer shows results that align with theory at two distinct fillings: $
u=2/7$ and $
u=2/9$. However, our new experiment on a single layer of PdSe$_2$ reveals significantly different behavior at $
u=2/7$ compared to $
u=2/9$. At $
u=2/7$, magnetorotons exhibit both chiral and reflection symmetry properties, whereas they displayed symmetry properties opposite to what was expected at $
u=2/9$. Our data further suggests the existence of two separate processes influencing magnetotronic effects: one based on charge transfer and the other on changing the moiré twist depth.

Our research explores the quick spread of an epidemic in a vast population where individuals interact in mass gatherings, examining dynamics on intricate networks that defy uniform analysis. Building upon previous work focusing on the dynamics of large, equally divided subgroups within uniform populations, we now generalize and simplify existing findings by relaxing certain assumptions, making the study more comprehensive and versatile. This expanded understanding enables us to accurately model and forecast the development of epidemics across diverse settings. Through our investigation, we have derived precise and easily applicable conclusions, shedding light on a wide range of epidemic scenarios. The final destination of our journey is a detailed evaluation of the critical thresholds that distinguish healthy populations from those on the brink of collapse, as well as an in-depth exploration of the intricate and multifaceted processes involved in large epidemics.

A strong point source in a CMB map strongly affects the error distribution 
when using a biased estimator due to its uncorrelated noise, leading to an 
imbalance in errors across the map. To mitigate this issue, an alternative 
estimator is developed with improved resilience to strong point sources and 
better Gaussian approximation properties, resulting in more uniform errors 
and a better signal-to-noise ratio. This new estimator is applied to the LFI CMB 
catalog to analyze its impact on recovering angular power spectra.

This paper suggests a task-based approach to instructing humans that draws on insights from education and pragmatism. By viewing task instruction as a learning process, we can develop more effective frameworks that incorporate key concepts like context, purpose, and demonstration. The proposed framework, called the Pedagogic Pragmatic Instructive (PPI) model, (1) establishes a clear context for the task, (2) identifies and sets specific goals, (3) provides a step-by-step guide with clear instructions, (4) offers hands-on practice with supportive materials, (6) conducts a thorough evaluation of the task outcome. The PPI model aims to facilitate more human-centered instruction, one that is grounded in both educational principles and practical considerations. To support this goal, we outline key design factors to ensure the success and efficiency of tasks and offer recommendations for future research.

Quantum state tomography typically requires unitary operations to gather information about a state, but some scenarios limit what operations can be applied to a known object, called the apparatus. This gives rise to shadow tomography, a technique that focuses on the known object and its effects on other states rather than the unknown state itself. Unlike traditional quantum state tomography, shadow tomography's outcome relies solely on the known object's effects, a concept studied in free probability theory. This work demonstrates how to extract a complete description of an unknown state from these effects through a specialized equation, and applies it to specific situations where the effects can be easily measured, such as certain quantum circuits. Additionally, it discusses strategies to gather relevant information about the unknown state even in scenarios where only a subset of these effects is accessible and considers the feasibility limits of doing so, all within the context of random unitary circuits.

The inradius and circumradius are fundamental concepts that reflect the size and spacing of convex shapes. To determine these radii, we typically need to know the shape's area and the length of a specific curve, which can be complicated to calculate. A recent study by Kallinen and Valovics provided a new method to estimate the inradius based on the distances between points on the shape's boundary. In this paper, we extend this idea to calculate the circumradius by modifying the underlying equation. Additionally, we demonstrate how the inradii of successive iterations of a shrinking shape converge to the circumradius, and these convergence rates are also examined. To apply these findings practically, we introduce a new approach for shrinking a polygon to a circle without the need for triangulation.

This research investigates the optimal path planning for multi-point multi-path UAV trajectories to maximize service delivery at locations with restricted UAV landing permissions, thus reducing unnecessary flight distances. By drawing a parallel with the orienteering problem, we formulate an efficient multi-path pathfinding model to maximize the coverage area of permitted UAV landing sites. To solve this model, we propose two algorithms: a precise but computationally intensive dynamic programming method and a efficient heuristic greedy algorithm that offers a trade-off between solution quality and computational complexity. Experimental results show that the proposed models and algorithms achieve significant distance reductions of up to 43.7% compared to baseline approaches, with only a 10% increase in computational time.

Research on the quantum phases of bilayer graphene has made notable advancements. A breakthrough discovery showed that bilayer graphene can transition into nematic and polar phases with low symmetry through the application of small electric fields. Studies have demonstrated the coexistence of these phases with a Landau level and the influence of lattice symmetry. The results indicate that nematic and polar states exhibit long-range correlations with the same symmetry as the underlying Dirac electrons. In contrast, the polar phase lacks intrinsic quantization and Hall responses, whereas the nematic and charge-density wave phases exhibit quantization and Hall responses characteristic of the Landau levels. The results also show that the rotational symmetry in the nematic state is broken while the translational symmetry remains intact. The findings suggest that the known nematic and charge-density wave phases of the Landau levels persist in the presence of an electric field.

When endoffullerenes are deposited onto a substrate, the intense van der Waals interactions cause a change in their shape. To gain insight into how this happens, researchers used molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the effects of different substrate conditions on the endofullerenes. The results of these studies can be utilized to predict the endofullerenes' magnetic and electric properties, as well as their optical properties, which are influenced by their changed shape due to intense van der Waals forces.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to widespread implications and profound effects on data collection across various settings, triggering heightened security and privacy concerns as a result. As conventional data storage methods are replaced by distributed and probabilistic data storage, which poses risks to sensitive data due to potential data breaches in decentralized systems or the drawing of adversarial samples in probabilistic systems, the need for an efficient and trusted data storage approach becomes pressing. Specifically, the problem of distributed probabilistic data storage, which combines distributed and probabilistic elements, is in urgent need of solution proposals. In light of these challenges, we introduce an innovative approach to this storage problem, proposing the use of multi-level, refined, and hierarchically structured data partitions, accompanied by the development of corresponding algorithms, to ensure secure and reliable data storage. Our system is designed to provide robust support for data update and query operations, while also allowing for efficient and adaptable data distribution as needed. A comprehensive evaluation framework is utilized to assess the proposed solution from multiple perspectives, including cost, security, and privacy, to ensure robustness and resilience. A thorough theoretical analysis and experimental study are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our system, with promising results highlighting its superior performance over existing state-of-the-art approaches.

To minimize errors and accelerate convergence in high-precision experiments, we apply Bayesian experiment design to optimize the measurement process. By comparing the outcomes of three different protocols - Bayesian, adaptive heuristic, and random - we demonstrate that the Bayesian approach yields results similar to adaptive heuristic protocols but significantly outperforms random ones. Notably, the Bayesian method surpasses adaptive protocols, ultimately producing the smallest uncertainty for a non-repeated measurement; interestingly, this strategy may not always lead to the shortest experimental duration but yields the most efficient measurement process when considering the information gained per unit of time. Our findings are particularly relevant for low-fidelity Ramsey measurements but can be generalized to other measurement types with linear relationships, such as optical interferometry, with potential applications in various scientific fields.

This paper explores how the concept of Gromov centrality can be applied to distinguish between self-similar networks, such as those with different dimensions. We apply the Gromov-mobility profile to a set of random and model-based networks, each with unique characteristics derived from previous research. The Gromov-mobility profile is generated by measuring the standard deviation of the degree distribution within a given neighborhood of each node. Our research demonstrates that the Gromov-mobility profile can effectively identify and distinguish between different types of networks, such as random and small-world networks, as well as networks with different dimensions. Additionally, we show that this approach can identify nodes with specific characteristics and highlight its potential for use in various network analysis applications.

Our cosmological theory, developed from the principles of dark matter and dark energy, incorporates a fundamental particle of negative mass, which we've dubbed the N-meson. This unique particle has properties that contrast significantly with those of regular matter. The Earth's rotation and orbit around the Sun are driven by negative mass flows, which also influence the Sun's movement within the galaxy. As negative mass contributes to the Sun's acceleration, a process known as dinamisism, we've observed an increase in the Earth-Sun distance over time. The Sun's acceleration rate has been precisely determined and found to be proportional to the galaxy's dark energy density, which further supports the dinamism process and suggests a possible future galactic collision. This potential collision, estimated to occur in approximately 36 million years, could be caused by the acceleration of the Sun's movement or a change in the galaxy's dark energy density.

We investigate various natural multivariate bundles of matrix polynomials whose spectral closure turns out to be open, revealing several factorization theorems in the process. These spectral bundles are characterized by certain matrix polynomial properties, parameterized by a matrix whose eigenvalues represent the spectral entity in question. For instance, the set of positive matrix polynomials, the set of matrix polynomials with nonpositive spectral norm, the set of matrix polynomials with nonnegative eigenvalues, and the set of matrix polynomials with a spectral radius less than one are examples of such bundles. Notably, the given families encompass more general cases - those with stricter spectral restrictions - and the set of matrix polynomials whose spectral radius is equal to one, including nilpotent matrix polynomials, is a special instance of these families as well.

The construction of continuous-trace algebras in their unitary and real forms plays a crucial role in exploring non-geometric T-dualities in string theory. We introduce a broader category of algebras known as continuous-trace algebras, which encompass previously studied continuous-trace groups as well as certain non-sovable continuous-trace groups. Calculations indicate that the classical T-duality of non-geometric Lee-Chang backgrounds can be realized on the real forms of sovable continuous-trace groups, whereas a general realization on unitary forms is also possible. Conversely, we demonstrate both theoretically and computationally that certain non-geometric T-dualities cannot be implemented within string theory based on Fock representations of continuous-trace algebras. Instead, we show that these limitations arise from the semi-simple 1-1 correspondence of the algebras and can be overcome by considering the duals of Fock representations of quantum deformation of the so-called "biproduct algebra" of the algebra.

Researchers have been exploring the computational intricacies of metric Baker's problems since the 1980s.  Recently, work by Saurabh and Sankowski yielded a $O(n^2 \log^2 n)$-time algorithm for the distance function enumeration problem, a breakthrough in efficiency.  Our research extends this achievement by introducing a novel embedding of the related concepts of submodular function and constraint satisfaction problems, allowing us to develop faster, $O(n^2)$-time algorithms for the distance function constraint satisfaction problem and related metric Baker's problems in graphs devoid of minor substructures.  This advance further enables the development of efficient single-source shortest paths queries with the $O(\sqrt{n})$ time complexity per query.  Our results can be attributed to the distinctive properties of the distance function, enabling the creation of sparse, hierarchical distance metric embeddings.  This area of computation remains an active area of research, with ongoing studies at MIT focused on expanding the applicability of these algorithms to graphs featuring only minor substructures.

This research paper investigates the distinct solutions and their stability when a given function $u$ is applied to a periodic parabolic equation with time-dependent periodic coefficients $\lambda$. By demonstrating that the set of solutions with positive prevalence dominates the set with negative prevalence through continuous parameter variations, we resolve the long-standing open problem of referring to solutions with positive prevalence as steady-state solutions. Furthermore, we examine the local and global stability of these prevailing solutions and investigate the exponent of the exponential decay rate in the stable manifold of the prevailing solution. This research is conducted within the framework of a bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ with $N \geq 2$.$\hspace{20cm} $

The adaptive quantum imaginary time evolution (ADAPT) variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) has demonstrated efficacy in computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the electronic Hamiltonian, specifically for large Gaussian-basis molecules on near-term hardware. Two distinct implementations, fermionic-ADAPT-VQE and qubit-ADAPT-VQE, were developed to compute eigenvalues using different computational paradigms, with the former employing fermionic qubits and the latter utilizing qubits in a fermionic encoding. By applying the quantum embedding approach, we developed the quantum embedding-ADAPT-VQE (QEB-ADAPT-VQE) protocol to compute eigenvalues within localized regions of the electronic spectrum. By applying a Fermi function to the computational cost function, we evaluated the computational cost and convergence speed of QEB-ADAPT-VQE, exhibiting improved efficiency and acceleration compared to both fermionic-ADAPT-VQE and qubit-ADAPT-VQE. Furthermore, we found that QEB-ADAPT-VQE can compute eigenvalues with higher accuracy than expected based on the computational budget, yielding superior precision compared to the original protocols.

A novel approach, the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), is presented as a flexible tool for visual analysis, which can be used with both labeled and unlabeled data. The DGD captures the underlying structure of complex datasets through a non-linear representation, modulating variations while preserving essential differences between classes when labeled data is provided. With unlabeled data, the DGD can automatically distinguish classes by identifying latent groupings from the representation, which can be done independently of visual visualization by encapsulating the representation process within a self-supervised Bayesian learning framework. As such, the DGD is well-suited for high-dimensional data analysis where visualization is challenging or ineffective. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the DGD in identifying non-linear sub-spaces that accurately classify lung nodules as benign or malignant and distinguish individual retinal vessels and drusen from artifacts.

We examine how introducing a near-vacuum string state with stiffness into the $w$CDM cosmological model affects the Hubble tension and the type Ia supernovae discrepancy.  Our analysis indicates that incorporating a near-vacuum string state with positive stiffness can resolve the Hubble tension and the discrepancy of type Ia supernovae, and similar results are observed for the additional tension between the Hubble constant and the cosmic microwave background polariation angle.  This near-vacuum string state, derived from string theory, can be approximated by an equation similar to the modified Maximon-Parker equation, and when considering only the leading term, can be represented by the equation $\left( \frac{\ddot{F}}{H \dot{F}} \right)_{\rm vac} = -3(1-w)$.  Assuming that the near-vacuum string state has negative energy density and that the variations in the string scale $F$ are small compared to 1, and further assuming that the string state starts to dominate at a redshift $z_{\rm d}$, can solve the Hubble tension and the discrepancy of type Ia supernovae when the parameter $F_0$ is sufficiently large.

Our research provides observations and analysis of gas emissions from a specific type of comet known as a frozen nucleus comet, utilizing data collected from the Submillimeter Array. Between April 2018 and April 2019, we tracked the emissions of eight molecules as the comet C/2015 ER61 made its approach, and we found significant acceleration in the emissions of most molecules except for HCN, which displayed distinct behavior when compared to other volatile emissions. By examining the emissions, we identified distinct phases and found that the emissions of some molecules, such as CS, H$_2$CO, HNC, and CH$_3$OH, exhibited similar patterns, suggesting they were released together at the same time, while HCN emissions started earlier and showed reduced activity. Our analysis of the emissions of highly volatile molecules, such as H$_2$O and H$_2$S, revealed that these molecules were released much earlier. Based on our findings, we developed a model that takes into account the emissions of volatile species, which were released in two distinct periods, and we found that the emissions of most molecules were released with similar velocities, except for HCN, which was released much faster. Our model also revealed that the emissions of highly volatile molecules were released much earlier and at a much higher velocity. The emergence of unsupervised speech synthesis through self-supervised learning (SSL) offers significant potential for model scalability, eliminating manual annotation needs, and broadening synthesis capabilities. Nonetheless, SSL's ability to produce high-quality speech, especially for complex tasks, has been limited thus far. In our study, we propose an adaptable yet efficient SSL framework for text-to-speech synthesis, incorporating a novel, compact variational autoencoder cross-entropy loss and an innovative, auto-regressive neural generator. In our experiments, our SSL model produced speech with comparable clarity and naturalness to its supervised counterpart, as evaluated using the F0, MEL-CCR, and FER for the TACOS dataset, and the automatic speech recognition, mean opinion score, and F0 metrics for the TACOS and Libri-light datasets, respectively.

We are examining a Tsallis holographic dark energy model with interaction between matter and dark energy, incorporating the time-dependent scale $R=t^{(1+n)/2}$ into the holographic dark energy equation. Assuming that the interacting model is at the Planck era, we derive the modified joint evolution law for $A(Q)$ and $B(Q)$ and derive the interacting coupling parameter $\xi(M)$ in terms of the constant parameter $n$ of the Tsallis model. We then analyze the geometric feature of the energy density and pressure of the interacting model by plotting the phase space portrait and root system, and determine the critical radius $R_{c}$ and corresponding energy density $\rho_{d}$ at the transition from the inflationary to the dark energy-dominated era for different values of $n$. Furthermore, we calculate the deceleration parameter $q$ and the effective gravitational constant $G_{eff}$ for various values of $n$ and discuss our results.

A new, simplified approach has been developed for comparing solution methodologies to well-defined optimization problems. The Investment Ratio (IR) metric effectively rates methods by considering their relative time and memory costs, enabling straightforward calculation directly from method outputs. This approach boasts versatility, allowing it to work with a range of problem types, including the currently studied De Bruijn graph application. The metric's validity is substantiated through the comparison of various parameter choices for the Fast Deletions problem.

In this paper, we explore the theoretical foundations of Geometric Singularity Theory within the framework of synthetic differential geometry. Building on the earlier work of Carbonneade and Pollan, we introduce the concepts of source path and source simply connected groupoid, before relating these to analytic notions via an adapted version of Mather's germ theory. Subsequently, we define key theoretical objects such as coranks, singularities, and $R$-points, before demonstrating their relevance to the existing literature through comparative analysis with Mather's work. Additionally, we prove that the geometric object constructed in this study corresponds to a Whittaker deformation space when applied to specific geometric scenarios.

The Dynaswap project is a multi-faceted study that integrates secure, distributed
infrastructure built on top of blockchain technology, incorporating secure smart contract
mechanisms, virtual machine deployments, and innovative workflow solutions powered by
flow-based programming techniques. This research demonstrates a SWAP contract execution
platform, showcasing an intelligent contract execution framework that facilitates dynamic
remediation and adaptive control flow adjustments. Furthermore, it introduces an intelligent
SWAP contract analysis tool, evaluating security and providing threat risk assessments. As
part of this research, the Dynaswap team has developed a SWAP contract integration
platform, integrating flow-based integration with blockchain smart contracts and also
examining the integration of traditional SWAP contracts with blockchain technology. This
platform's development showcases the potential of SWAP contracts in finance and trade, as
well as the existing challenges in their integration with blockchain infrastructure. Additionally,
the Dynaswap team has created a SWAP contract management platform, demonstrating the
potential integration of blockchain smart contracts with management tools and solutions. As
part of this research, the Dynaswap team has created a SWAP trading platform, integrating
blockchain smart contracts with trading infrastructure and also presenting the potential
of SWAP trading within blockchain smart contract infrastructure. This research also showcases
