Research on silicene nanor ribbons decorated with Mn atoms from both its sublattice sites has been analyzed to understand the impact of this decoration on the electronic properties of silicene. Calculations based on tight-binding models and the density functional theory have identified the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter as being significantly affected by the decoration site. Specifically, it has been found that decorating the sublattice site with two Mn atoms per site yields an onsite Hubbard interaction parameter of approximately 1.3 eV, which aligns with the value obtained from density functional theory, in contrast to the decoration of the top site which yields an onsite Hubbard interaction parameter of approximately 1.0 eV. It has also been found that within- and inter-sublattice interactions can be tuned to be either repulsive or attractive depending on the decoration site, which has implications for the ferromagnetic half-semiconductor half-metal transition in silicene nanoribbons decorated with Mn atoms.

The galactic centre region Sgr A East, a molecular complex near Earth's sun's distance from the galactic centre, is shrouded in dust and observed to emit extremely weak radio waves and X-rays, with some speculating that it might be a molecular ring surrounding a supermassive black hole. To understand what Sgr A East consists of, researchers used a technique called spectral energy distribution fitting to analyze radio and X-ray data. Their findings suggest that Sgr A East contains a molecular core with massive molecular molecules and a thin layer of gas. With further examination of its radio waves and X-rays, they discovered a ring of molecular compounds and a possible molecular core, concluding that Sgr A East consists of a dense molecular core and a thin layer of gas. These results support the idea that Sgr A East is indeed a molecular core at a distance of about 8 parsecs from the galactic centre.

This paper investigates the KNN and SVM algorithms' resilience to overfitting when dealing with class imbalance issues using C-modified variants. We compare the performance of these algorithms with ResNet, a neural network, also trained on C-modified versions of the imbalanced data. Our study considers two measures of class imbalance: a relatively minor discrepancy in the number of samples (e.g. 60\%-40\%) and an extreme disparity (e.g. 98\%-2\%). The results show that overfitting significantly affects KNN and SVM but has a relatively minor impact on ResNet. Consequently, using C-modified variants does not yield substantial improvements in the accuracy of KNN and SVM but substantially boosts the accuracy of ResNet. The research suggests that oversampling the minority class exacerbates the overfitting issue in KNN, SVM, and ResNet, whereas undersampling the majority class has the opposite effect in KNN and SVM but a limited effect on ResNet. Ultimately, simply training ResNet on imbalanced data tends to produce higher accuracy than KNN and SVM, even without using C-modified variants.

This paper examines how journalists covered the COVID-19 pandemic in 31 countries between 2019 and 2020, focusing on news outlets' initial response, volume, and content. Using a machine translation system, the study analyzed 1,535 articles from 31 countries and gathered data on local news coverage, enabling a comparative analysis of national and international news patterns. Results indicate both countries and individual news outlets exhibited distinct news patterns. A significant decline in local news volume was observed in March 2020, after which international news became more prominent in local news coverage, particularly regarding COVID-19 updates. Moreover, the study found that local news content was primarily comprised of government announcements and health updates, with a minimal incorporation of international news on this topic.

We have integrated the Fast Multipole Method into the N-body integration routine of the N-Body ToolKit, previously developed by Nathaniel R. Badcock, to accelerate the computation of gravitational interactions in astrophysical simulations. By implementing FMM, which approximates far-field interactions, we have reduced the time complexity of computing the force on each particle from O(N) to O(N log*N) for distant particles, thereby achieving significant speedups in tasks such as orbit determinations and collision detection. We have tested N-Body ToolKit with FMM on various scenarios including planetary systems, star clusters, and galaxy collisions, and found it to be stable and accurate with a high precision of 10^-12 for particles with up to 100,000 neighbors. The incorporation of FMM has greatly improved the tool's performance, with a typical speedup of 5-10 times for scenarios with many distant particles.

The HeliPol collaboration has proposed evaluating the polarized structure function $g_1(x,Q^2)$ using the electron-proton-positron collision data for the process $\mathrm{e} \mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{e} \mathrm{P}$ in collider experiments. The study evaluated the double spin asymmetry in an alternative process $\mathrm{e} \mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{e} \mathrm{P}$ and explored its potential to determine the structure function $g_1(x,Q^2)$ for kinematic conditions where the proton's target spin polarization is zero. The structure $g_1(x,Q^2)$ was extracted from the double spin asymmetry measurements, demonstrating the feasibility of the $\mathrm{e} \mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{e} \mathrm{P}$ process for determining this structure function. The proposed $\mathrm{e} \mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{e} \mathrm{P}$ method could be an efficient alternative to the more traditional $\mathrm{e} \mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{e} \mathrm{q}$ scattering for investigating the polarized structure function $g_1(x,Q^2)$.

In complex high-dimensional control issues, transferring knowledge of an expert to a student is a difficult task. Traditional policy cloning methods, which treat the student and expert policies as identical, become impractical when the control space becomes too large. However, a new approach, augmented policy cloning, enables the student to learn an optimized control pattern similar to the expert's, which can be viewed as a localized version of the expert policy. This study develops a novel method to create an augmented space for policy cloning and applies it to robotic reaching tasks. Furthermore, the method allows for identifying and ignoring irrelevant dimensions during cloning, which can significantly reduce processing time. The proposed approach also enables simultaneous learning of the relevant control dimensions of both the student and expert policies. The results demonstrate that augmented policy cloning can effectively transfer knowledge from an expert to a student in a reaching task with a large number of irrelevant dimensions.

Studies investigating the production of Higgs bosons via gluon fusion have been analyzed using data collected by the ATLAS detector at 13 TeV from 2015 to 2018, totaling 139 inverse femtobarns. Data on the $HH$ decay mode, comprising $W$-boson pairs, have been examined to identify and isolate resonance signals from background sources. A range of mass hypotheses, between 220 and 345 GeV for a heavy scalar and between 240 and 315 GeV for a heavy pseudoscalar, was explored. These analyses did not find evidence for excesses above background levels, resulting in 95% confidence level upper limits on $HH$ production in the 21-45% and 25-55% ranges for scalar and pseudoscalar resonances, respectively. Additionally, data from 7 TeV and 8 TeV ATLAS searches were used to set constraints on $HH$ production in heavy scalar and pseudoscalar resonances, yielding upper limits of 35% and 40-60%, respectively.

Research on resonant spin maser systems has experienced a resurgence due to a
combination of theoretical and experimental breakthroughs. To advance and refine
this investigation, we suggest an innovative method of analyzing the behavior
of digital signal processing within resonant spin maser systems. We have created
a new framework, known as the spin-photon cat boson space, in which the key
components of these systems are easily understood within a unified context. By
integrating concepts from quantum information and maser physics, this
generalized framework provides straightforward interpretations of crucial processes
such as amplification, filtering, and quantum state manipulation. Furthermore,
we demonstrate how to apply quantum interference in the spin-photon cat boson
space to enhance the performance of resonant spin maser systems based on a few
key parameters. Notably, this approach allows for improved sensitivity and output
power, achieving super-Standard-Three-Sided-Coin performance with minimal noise.

In a specific context, certain groups can be used to analyze symmetries of a particular type of mathematical surface, known as a K3 surface. By categorizing all possible groups of this type, regardless of whether they arise from this context or not, we can make progress in understanding certain problems in number theory. Our key finding is the creation of a comprehensive, structured system, called a hypergeometric group, which can be used to represent many of these groups in a more predictable way. As a result, we can identify patterns and relationships among them. This framework also allows us to re-examine the groups associated with K3 surfaces that have multiple reflecting reflections and demonstrates their connection to the groups associated with certain periodic elliptic surfaces.

We propose a novel experimental approach to identify a cold dark matter candidate in a lab setting. Our analysis focuses on the scenario where a visible sector neutralino decays into a hidden sector neutralino and a photon, and is feasible with current IZIP experiment technology. Leveraging LHC data and IZIP search results, we can establish a lower bound on the lifetime of the visible sector neutralino based on its mass. Our study further extends to low-mass dark matter scenarios, including fermions and bosons, and reveals the constraints on the Yukawa coupling and mass ratio derived from LHC searches. Building on the LHC discovery of the Higgs-like boson, we assume its decoupling with heavy dark matter. Finally, we outline a possible LHC IZIP search and a lab-based beam experiment to detect the decay neutralino -> hidden neutralino gamma.

The genus of a graph G is defined as the minimum number of required surfaces needed for an embedding of G to be achieved. We will provide two definitions, one using Euler characteristics and another using the signature of a 4-manifold, both of which we will prove to be equivalent. We will also establish that the genus function can be extended to any weighted graph when its absolute weighted genus remains greater than or equal to 2, and this result can be further applied to any graph when its genus is greater than or equal to its number of loops plus 1. With these new findings, we will resolve two long-standing problems, namely the Abelian Tucker conjecture and the generalized genus conjecture for weighted graphs.

We can refine two communi- cation-intensive stochastic optimization techniques, namely Stochastic Gradient Dyadic Computation (SGDC) and Stochastic Variance-Reduced Method (SVRM), by reducing their communication efforts while maintaining convergence properties. Building on mini-batch strategies, these optimized methods, dubbed mini-SGDC and mini-SVRM, can be implemented in a distributed setting with a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{K}\right)$. Notably, by leveraging variance reduction techniques and incorporating expert feedback, these methods achieve performance equivalence to local stochastic gradient descent (LSGD) and local variance-reduced SGD (LVR-SGD) in a fully-distributed context, all within a single communication round. Furthermore, by optimizing communication rounds, these optimized methods can maintain faster convergence rates. For instance, by performing $K$ iterations and $n$ mini-batches per iteration, mini-SGDC and mini-SVRM can achieve a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/n \log (K/n)\right)$. We also present numerical evidence demonstrating the efficacy of these optimized methods.

Our research explores the effectiveness of transfer learning in multilingual model training. To achieve this, we compare the performance of language models, both with and without transfer learning, across 26 African languages, taking into account the level of linguistic relatedness and shared history among these languages. The results indicate that transfer learning yields enhanced training outcomes for languages with common origins, but may even hinder model training when dealing with linguically distinct languages. This phenomenon, we find, is largely attributed to the mutual interference and competition for common features within multilingual datasets, which can be mitigated by controlling the level of linguistic relatedness among the languages in question. Ultimately, our study sets the stage for future investigations into the mechanisms governing transfer learning in multilingual model training, with a particular focus on the complexities of low- and medium-resource languages, particularly those spoken across the African continent.

The performance of the current GTPC detector recoil event identification can be enhanced by incorporating two newly introduced observables. These are calculated from particle tracks within the detector and provide differences in electron-nucleon scattering that are not accounted for by existing methods. A study using a simplified simulation comparable to DarkSide-20in found that the addition of these observables improved the differentiation between electron and nuclear recoils, particularly in terms of their purity and efficiency. Furthermore, the experiment observed no statistically significant evidence of WIMPs using a simplified analysis and experiment conditions similar to DarkSide-20in.

The evaluation of driver behavior is typically confined to metrics such as acceleration and distance following. However, these standard metrics may not be sufficient to fully understand performance in complex driving situations, such as navigating roundabouts and merging with traffic. To improve assessments, we developed a method that incorporates human oversight. First, we created a system to automatically extract driver behavior metrics from vehicle data. Then, we designed a framework to integrate human input, allowing experts to identify suboptimal behavior in automated driving system (ADS) routes and assign labels to corresponding road features. This process enhances the accuracy of ADS behavior simulation and provides more detailed insights into driver behavior. Our research demonstrates that human oversight enhances the prediction of driver behavior and gives more detailed insights into driver behavior.

The task of reading text in images has seen significant progress since 2017, but a major issue still affects its performance: when the model encounters text it has not seen before during training, it struggles to read it. A major part of making neural networks good at reading text in images involves training them on a special dataset that includes a wide variety of text, so they can handle when they encounter new text, and this dataset is a crucial part of the progress made in this area of computer vision. This study proposes an approach to reading text in images that uses a large dataset of unseen text, and shows how it helps the process by providing a bigger pool of characters to learn from. A major part of the proposed approach involves using a part of the seen dataset that includes text symbols, and another part that includes images of text to help the model learn reading text in images. Experiments show the benefits of this approach, and the study's knowledge dataset can help to advance the performance of computer vision models.

Two-dimensional random fields displaying complex, irregular patterns are frequently observed in various disciplines, including turbulence research and scientific simulations.  Random fields with this characteristic can be modeled using two distinct statistical distributions: one representing "smooth" variations at short ranges and another describing "wild" fluctuations at longer ranges.  This paper proposes a numerical approach to evaluate the similarity between two separate random fields following different statistical models.  Two methodologies are presented: the first relies on calculating a similarity score using a series of pairwise comparisons between fields randomly cropped from each respective field, and the comparison of these two scores is used to determine the similarity between the fields.  The second method, drawing on ideas from machine learning, involves categorizing pairs of randomly selected field values into separate groups based on their respective underlying distributions, and then measuring the similarity between the fields based on the likelihood that their locally sampled pairs fall within the correctly labeled category.  Our tests with mock data from two specific models demonstrate that both techniques effectively identify patterns of similarity and difference, although the second method generally performs better and also offers advantages in terms of computational efficiency and the potential to tackle more complex random field models.

The technique of magnetic levitation is being utilized to study fluid dynamics without physical support for the plates. Research is particularly focused on evaluating the influence of suspended plates on the initial conditions of experiments involving plate tectonics. The plates used in this study are made from 2mm thick stainless steel and shaped like discs or squares, with an area of approximately 8cm in diameter or 12cm in length. Magnetic levitation enables the creation of varied magnetic fields and the achievement of a stable, horizontal position. The stability of the plates relies on the equilibrium of two opposing magnetic forces and their torsional rigidity. The experiments conducted thus far involve observing the plates using high-speed cameras under still or flowing air conditions, with an air flow created by the oscillation of a nearby magnet. The plates exhibit complex movements including oscillations, rotation, bending, and detachment from the support, with some detached plates hovering in mid-air. A high-speed camera captures the intricate plate dynamics in still or dynamic environments. The outcomes of these experiments include a vast array of motions that the plates exhibit, providing initial conditions for further dynamic analysis. The results of these experiments indicate that magnetic levitation offers great potential for the simulation of diverse plate configurations and initial conditions in still or dynamic environments.

Let's consider the symplectic group Spn(Z), which is a direct extension of SL2(Z) and SO2n+1(R). We define Hecke L-functions for primitive forms within the Hilbert-Mumford stratification and find these functions have analytic continuation within a specific region, bounded by the bosonic Siegel space and a compact space at infinity. These L-functions possess SL2(Z) analogues as cuspidal Hecke eigenforms, yet exhibit distinct behavior, such as L-functions becoming zero on the real axis for Spn(Z) forms without Siegel cusp. Utilizing the Poincaré bundle and Hilbert-Mumford stratification, we construct Hecke eigenforms within any given Hilbert-Mumford stratum and develop a procedure for investigating integral representations of the L-functions across all Hecke eigenforms within a stratum, extending prior work of Iwaniec, Luo, Mortula, and Wang for SL2(Z) L-functions.

To analyze graphene and normal conductor junctions, a single mode network, based on a scattering theory using the Green functions of non-interacting systems, is developed. Assuming self-consistent equilibrium state, the developed theory naturally includes the influence of contact resistance, leading to a well-defined graphene's intrinsic transport characteristics, unaffected by contact resistance. The transport quantities in graphene exhibit significantly different electronic structures compared to traditional conductors. Applying this theory to a series of normal graphene junctions, finite chains of different lengths, where the junctions' properties are determined by tight-binding model, reveals that the contact resistance cannot be neglected even for short chains. The developed theory is also applicable to junctions of graphene and superconductors, allowing for the calculation of critical current and other transport characteristics. These findings provide a solid basis for the study of transport quantities in graphene and carbon nanotree junctions, facilitating the solution of transport related problems.

The present research aims to derive fast convergence rates for meromorphic approximation on various Banach lattices in several complex variables, employing the method of topological divisors. It extends previous work, leveraging the properties of weakly nonlinear and weakly monotone operators to establish convergence in diverse norms. The findings are illustrated through multiple examples, showcasing the complexity and variability of the resulting operators. Additionally, the paper identifies new challenges and obstacles arising from operator theory that necessitate the innovative use of divisors to tackle approximation problems.

We investigate the properties of pancyclic graphs with large minimum degree in the given range greater than or equal to $n^{\alpha}$ where $0.166<n^{\alpha}<0.5$. It is demonstrated that if such a graph has vertices $n$, then its maximum number of non-cyclic components is $n$ minus $0.5n^{\alpha+1}+O(n)$, and a pancyclic graph with minimum degree greater than or equal to $n^{\alpha}$ has at most $n$ cycles of length $3$ and $4$. This leads to the conclusion that for $n$ sufficiently large and $0.166<n^{\alpha}<0.5$, a pancyclic graph with minimum degree greater than or equal to $n^{\alpha}$ has vertices at least $n/\phi$, where $\phi$ is the golden ratio. This improves the previously existing results. The same set of conditions enables us to show that a pancyclic graph with minimum degree greater than or equal to $n^{\alpha}$ has an independence number not greater than $n/2.5$ if $n$ is sufficiently large.

The initial conditions of the medium play a significant role in understanding how light hadrons are produced and transported. By expanding on the hydrodynamic description in the initial phase, we demonstrate that a softer initial medium leads to a steeper pressure gradient, reduced flow velocity, and lower source strength compared to a denser medium. Consequently, the predicted yields of mesons are less affected by the initial conditions than previously assumed. Notably, certain initial profiles can even result in negative pressure gradients below a certain threshold in momentum, leading to accelerated instead of decelerated flow. Our research supports the idea that a softer initial medium could contribute to the observed higher flow velocities in most peripheral collisions.

To enhance the accuracy of the spectral SASK approach, we introduce a system of
modified PDEs that tightly approximates the original equations. This innovative
PDE system, termed PDSASK, allows for an increased flexibility in the choice of
expansion spaces for approximating PDSASK's solutions. Our analysis of PDSASK
focuses on a specific combination of spaces that can be efficiently solved to yield a
highly efficient and robust solver for the original partial differential equations.

We employed a multi-configurational self-consistent-field method with spherical symmetry to study a water molecule in a strong DC electric field. Our calculations showed highly accurate agreement with quantum-electrodynamics-based results, as well as refined estimates of resonances, notably in determining the rotationally adjusted frequencies of dipole-type resonances, which were overcorrected, yielding more precise values than previously reported for $\tilde{A}_1$. Additionally, we investigated the influence of various basis sets on their convergence and found that a moderately sized aug-cc-pV5Z basis set in conjunction with a 60-point grid for the Legendre basis yields sufficient accuracy for the calculation of resonances in the high-frequency regime. Our study further provides explicit coefficients from the MCSCF wave function, which can be used in subsequent calculations.

The Sinkhorn algorithm is commonly used for solving the Sinkhorn-Knopp problem, a cotraction-free solution to the Schrödinger problem. When the Schrödinger problem doesn't have a solution, or no approximate solution, the Sinkhorn algorithm still operates by default. In such cases, the algorithm either enters an infinite loop or orients itself towards a cotraction-free setting. For instance, when dealing with an over-determined system where the solution set is empty, the Sinkhorn algorithm explores all possible non-matrices. Conversely, when dealing with an under-determined system where the solution set is infinite, the algorithm enters a loop. Furthermore, when dealing with equations rather than inequalities, the algorithm enters a loop. Lastly, when the limiting diaspora measure doesn't exist, the algorithm enters a loop.

Measurements of the proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider at CERN of 5.02 TeV center-of-mass energy are presented for top-quark pair production. The analysis is based on data collected by the CMS experiment, totaling 27.4 inverse femtobarns of luminosity. By evaluating the differential cross-sections of top-quark pair events in terms of top-quark transverse momentum, dilepton mass, and negative rapidity, both in the transverse momentum and mass distributions, a comparison is made with next-to-leading order quantum chromodynamics predictions, incorporating precision electroweak calculations and top-quark pole mass predictions. The results demonstrate consistency between these measurements and theoretical predictions, including those determined using the top-quark pole mass and the top-quark pole mass over top-quark mass relation for fixing the electroweak parameter $\mtop$.

The study of quantum systems impacted by classical noise has significant implications for understanding the behavior of quantum measurements in various scenarios. Disregarding the environment typically leads to uncontrolled decoherence in isolated quantum systems. In contrast, including the surroundings can clarify the effects of disorder on quantum correlations within a closed quantum system. This study examines the entanglement between a central quantum unit and surrounding repetitive spin chains that are interacting with each other under the influence of random noise. The results reveal that the quantum connections between these systems and their surroundings reach a stable equilibrium state and can be precisely calculated. The findings are verified by analyzing the long-term behavior of entanglement in different types of disorder and their impact on the central quantum unit. The results also demonstrate that the rate at which the central quantum unit loses coherence due to random noise depends on the specific type of disorder present. The research involves developing a set of equations that describe the behavior of quantum systems with multiple components interacting with each other under the influence of random noise, as well as experimentally verifying the results using data from a central qubit that is connected to surrounding repetitive chains of superconducting flux qubits.

This research aims to derive several necessary and sufficient conditions for a modified Bessel function of the first kind, extended with complex parameters, to exhibit Janowski convexity and starlikeness properties within the unit disk.

The COVID-19 pandemic, the most severe global crisis since 9/11, led to an unprecedented increase in deaths worldwide, surpassing 3.5 million people, and left lasting impacts on economies, healthcare systems, and social structures. Our analysis focuses on the initial phase (February 2020 to November 2021) of the pandemic, covering 150 countries, and examines its effects on urban areas, revealing increased reliance on remote work, elevated air pollution levels, and reduced diversity of urban encounters. Moreover, our research findings show that more affluent cities better navigated the crisis, while smaller cities, particularly those in developing nations, struggled to adapt and ultimately experienced enhanced long-term resilience and diversity of urban encounters but at a great human cost.

Current methods for solving multi-scale multi-physical mass transport and air quality models are often inefficient due to high computational costs. A new approach, FSMSN, is presented as a high-order time-advective solver using a fully-implicit method with space and time adaptive grid refinement. This algorithm stands out from traditional methods, such as the Sequential Fully Implicit method, by solving multiple physical processes simultaneously rather than sequentially. As a result, FSMSN efficiently handles the complex interactions between different physical processes, minimizing computational overhead. A fundamental component of FSMSN is its non-linear iterative solver, which ensures the consistency of multiple physical solutions at each time step. Furthermore, FSMSN employs an advanced non-stiff time integration scheme, MOLTOV, that utilizes an arbitrary-order filter to solve the non-linear equations. A novel feature of FSMSN is its ability to efficiently handle multiple physical processes with different time scales through a semi-implicit approach. This method solves temperature and chemical species equations iteratively while keeping velocity and pressure static between iterations. A fundamental numerical scheme adopted by FSMSN is the Nonlinearly Implicit High Order Vortex Bounded Method, which efficiently handles the solution of multiple physical processes interacting with complex grid structures. A fundamental solution framework adopted by FSMSN is the sequential solution of velocity, temperature, and chemical species equations, with iterative solutions of multiple physical equations at each time step. The inherent singularity of a one-handedness chiral optical cavity greatly amplifies the coupling between circularly polarized light and localized chiral quantum emitters. By properly aligning the cavity and emitter handedness, the emitters' interactions with light are greatly amplified, resulting in a highly enhanced spontaneous emission rate. The phenomenon is characterized by two distinct emission rates, one for each circular polarization state, leading to a complete modulation of emission when the emitter is positioned near the cavity's center. The emitter's resonance frequency can be finely adjusted by varying the adjacent metal plate's distance. The proposed single-handedness chiral optical cavity has the potential to efficiently enhance the emitters' interaction with left-handed circularly polarized light, making it an ideal tool for detecting and manipulating enantiomer differences at the molecular level, particularly in the presence of ambient right-handed light.

Two-dimensional anti-de-Sitter spaces are the semi-classical form of two-dimensional string theory and have no positive weight states in their Hilbert space. This leads to the possibility that all scattering states are in the semi-classical form, resulting in a state known as minimal string theory. A crucial aspect of this theory is the evaluation of string partition functions, which can then be used to determine the central charge and the c-function. By employing the FZZ boundary state approach and using the dual holographic description given by the Poincaré patch of anti-de-Sitter space, we calculate the partition functions for minimal string theory. This is done by expressing the FZZ boundary state in terms of creation and annihilation operators of a primary state with lowest energy, then using the Virasoro algebra's commutation relations to find the desired partition functions.

Researchers investigating the Alcubierre warp drive have re-examined the mathematics behind this concept, with a focus on achieving a stable warp bubble without requiring exotic matter. Their study differentiates between matter that is stationary and that in motion, with impressive results: stable warp bubbles can be achieved with either type of matter or energy configurations. In the case of stationary matter, specific conditions have been identified that prevent singularities and allow a stable warp bubble. Conversely, matter in motion may produce a stable warp bubble through a process resembling thrust. Notably, all these solutions satisfy the requirement for negative energy within the warp bubble, but fulfill the condition of positive energy at the edge. The new solutions significantly reduce the amount of negative mass required, making such warp bubbles both feasible and realistic.

The management of urban infrastructure is becoming increasingly complex due to
expanding cities and the rising demands on existing systems. Effective
decision-making is hindered by limited data availability, high data
collection costs, and the difficulty in gathering information from diverse
stakeholders. To address these challenges, we present GUIDES, an integrated
decision-support framework for managing urban underground infrastructure.
Comprising both physical and digital components, GUIDES aims to provide real
time traffic monitoring and optimized traffic flow management in urban roads.
A key aspect of the framework is its ability to balance the needs of various
stakeholders in urban underground spaces, enabling optimal resource
allocation across different infrastructure layers.

A two-dimensional Coulomb crystal formed from 199Hg$^{+}$ ions in a Penning trap has been analyzed for its dependence on ambient temperature. By leveraging the trap's magnetic field gradient to determine the ions' positions, the spatial distribution of the two-dimensional array can be used to calculate the ambient heating rate. Experiments indicate that the initial heating of the crystal is consistent at 2 K/s, which is significantly higher than the predicted value of 0.5 K/s according to the established theoretical model. Several potential explanations for the observed discrepancy have been presented.

Tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy combines electromagnetic and chemical effects, allowing researchers to break speed and spatial limits in measurement techniques. A new computational model has been suggested to interpret tip-enhanced Raman spectra, specifically considering how the electromagnetic and chemical effects interact. This model can account for specific Raman band intensities and lineshapes, providing insight into the role of each effect in different measurement conditions. A key assumption behind this model is the presence of two types of tips, each with distinct properties, allowing researchers to accurately interpret measurements by comparing data from different tips. By applying this model, researchers can determine the role of the electromagnetic effect in different measurement conditions and how the chemical effect can be enhanced for more precise measurements. This will help researchers to combine the strengths of the electromagnetic and chemical effects in tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, making this technique even more powerful in various applications.

Our previous study (Arancona et al. 2018) identified three spiral galaxies with prominent metal-poor stellar halos, which served as ideal candidates to search for the signatures of Accreted Multiple Populations (AME) through photometric analysis. Although the galactic halos contained younger stars with similar properties to those found in their respective inner disks, our previous findings raised several doubts due to the lack of clear spatial distribution data of these populations. In this current research, we aim to search for the AME in these three galaxies by using Hubble Space Telescope data of their inner regions. Our analysis involved examining wavelength-dependent color differences between multiple metallicity populations in two galaxies, NGC 1019 and NGC 5850, which did not display distinct spatial distribution patterns. In contrast, our findings suggest that the AME is present in NGC 1019, which exhibits homogeneous conditions for multiple population formation similar to that observed in NGC 5128. On the other hand, our data failed to demonstrate the presence of AME in NGC 5850, which may be due to either the absence of accreted matter or the limited visibility of such a component. In conclusion, our research indicates that searching for the AME in metal-poor stellar halos of spiral galaxies requires the presence of multiple population components with distinct spatial distribution patterns and homogeneous metallicity properties.

A microcalorimeter was used to examine the high-pressure entropy changes associated with the phase transitions in ammonium sulfate and potassium nitrate. For ammonium sulfate, the entropy changes measured were consistent with results from high-pressure X-ray diffraction and neutron diffraction experiments, indicating that the entropy increase upon transitioning to the ferroelectric state is primarily due to the polar sublattice. For potassium nitrate, the entropy changes measured were not in agreement with results from high-pressure X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy experiments, suggesting that the employed microcalorimeter may introduce systematic errors.

Research suggests that humans, on average, tend to play it safe in probability games, choosing the most likely outcome over higher-stakes possibilities. Meanwhile, learning theories attribute this behavior to individuals' sensitivity to recent losses or their ability to adjust to changing probabilities. We developed a global network model of the learning process that explains average behavior in such games. In this model, information about probabilities is stored in separate neural pathways that interact and influence each other. According to our analysis, the tendency to engage in probability-matching can be attributed to the degree of integration or separation of these pathways in response to negative outcomes. By examining statistical patterns in real-life decision-making data, we were able to simulate the underlying neural structure and test the accuracy of our model. The results confirmed that our global network model accurately predicts a key characteristic of human learning behavior.

The concepts of nonlocality and contextuality are intertwined, yet distinct aspects of quantum mechanics that are difficult to quantify. We developed a method to compare the levels of nonlocality and contextuality present in different quantum state configurations by defining two indices. These indices, calculated from the geometric algebra of the algebra representing the quantum system, are fundamental properties of the algebra's geometry. We applied this method to analyze experiment designs for simple systems, such as qubits, and found that nonlocality and contextuality can switch on in different combinations, depending on the states and queries used in the experiment. This unique ability, called state reconfigurability, is crucial for understanding diverse conceptually different nonlocal and contextual effects present in different systems.

We focus on the near neighbor problem for vector spaces with a large number of dimensions. Our approach develops a method to efficiently solve this problem by approximating a dataset with a much simpler, smaller equivalent. This result is achieved through a newly identified connection between the problems of approximating nearest neighbors and clustering. Our technique enables us to maintain a relatively small approximation factor by regularly updating the approximation dataset, ensuring that it accurately represents the original data with minimal error. This results in significant improvements over previous methods in several ways: Firstly, our approach can reduce the time complexity by up to 1 minus a small negative value. Secondly, our ability to update the dataset allows for a 1 over n^3/2 minus a small negative power times more efficient handling of queries. Lastly, all while preserving an accurate approximation, which does not rely on any specific assumption about the data. This is achieved through a novel application of several advanced techniques from the fields of probability, statistics, information theory and combinatorics.

Currently, learning the inverse process using neural networks is the main method for unfolding and mitigating measurement errors on quantum computers. However, the practical application of this technique is restricted by the large number of outputs it can only handle efficiently. A recently suggested approach, which involves using Bayesian unfolding in combination with a parameterizing filter, has the potential to be more efficient but requires more complex statistical processing. However, by breaking this statistical processing down into smaller iterative steps, researchers have now developed a more scalable version of the method. This new version involves two stages: the first involves learning the inverse process, which can be handled efficiently by the neural network, and the second involves applying a Bayesian unfolding technique using a parameterized filter. This step is performed iteratively and each iteration can be handled more efficiently as it involves a progressively narrower distribution. This more scalable version of the method has now been successfully tested using data from a superconducting quantum system.

To understand robots' behavior during sequence-based tasks like cooking, humans need access to the robots' decision-making process. Current approaches involve using the robots' action history to predict their future behavior, but this information is often incomplete. A new study examines how humans learn from a robot's actions and whether humans can infer the robots' task input mapping by analyzing their actions. The research found that humans can easily deduce a robot's chosen task input when following the robots' action history, resulting in significantly decreased efficiency. To address this issue, the study proposes a method called Partial-HMM that enables robots to hide their decision-making process by only providing limited information about their action history. The results show that by giving humans limited information about the robots' action history, humans' efficiency increases and they are less likely to deduce the robots' task input mapping.

Global metric maps like OctoMap effectively navigate complex environments by incorporating uncertainty metrics to handle sensor limitations. However, their computation is restricted to real-time data and becomes slow when processing historical data due to the map's 3D quadtree/Priority-Flood structure. In contrast, simple histogram-based methods like Topological Occupancy Map (TOP) provide fast computation but lack the accuracy needed for reliable robot navigation. To integrate the benefits of both, we propose HiTMap, a new representation that combines the navigation features of global maps with the speed of histogram-based methods. Specifically, HiTMap uses a dynamic structure to encode occupancy values as multi-dimensional vectors, where each dimension corresponds to a time interval and power of two. By scaling power values, we ensure that HiTMap is equally suitable for maps with few or many data points, enabling seamless integration of real-time and historical data. Furthermore, the vector representation facilitates efficient computation of various map operations, such as distance metrics and vector arithmetic. Our evaluation demonstrates that HiTMap is effective in outdoor scenarios using real data, while simulations show its superiority over Top and OctoMap.

Research on constructing 2-D Z-complementary array code sets (ZACs) using generalized Boolean functions has been conducted, and a method for creating Z-complementary array code sets (ZACs) in two dimensions by employing generalized Boolean functions has been established. Unlike traditional Boolean functions used for this purpose, the underlying functions here can have affine terms over any number of variables. It has been found that there exist ZACs with sizes exceeding those produced by the best-known Boolean functions used for this purpose. Additionally, a set of optimal ZACs, known as optimal Z-complementary array code sets (oZACs), has been derived from the proposed general Boolean functions.

A novel learning approach for CT image reconstruction is introduced to tackle the limitations imposed by non-Gaussian data distribution and excessive radiation in CT scans. Leveraging the capabilities of Generative Adversarial Networks in modeling non-Gaussian data distribution, a comprehensive CT image reconstruction model is developed, capable of simultaneously removing artifacts and compensating for the excessive radiation. Through the incorporation of residual learning techniques, the proposed model is designed to address the diverse range of noise levels encountered in CT imaging, facilitated by a multi-task discriminator with two networks. Experimental results from the Data Challenge on Generative Adversarial Networks demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model over traditional CT image reconstruction methods.

The effect of gaps in finite periodic structures on light propagation is analyzed and compared to predictions made by both the effective medium theory and a local approach. It's found that the effective medium theory is more accurate than the local model, yet the local model's inaccuracies provide insight into the location and size of the gaps. Building upon this, a refined model incorporating these findings is developed and shows better agreement with both the effective medium theory and numerical simulations than the local model alone. This enhanced model accounts for a specific "effective gap width" that considers multiple scattered fields and demonstrates that light propagation can be described through the interplay of higher-order terms. Notably, this model's effectiveness is independent of the type of light source used. To confirm these findings, a series of experiments was performed on a 2D photonic crystal and the results demonstrate that the model's predictions are applicable in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional contexts.

Contextual Named Entity Retrieval aims to gather user feedback to enhance entity selection, leveraging context from text passages and user input in conjunction with relevance to improve contextual understanding. The process involves combining extracted entities from multi-label microservices to generate a list of potential candidates, ultimately ranking entities based on relevance. The system utilizes contextual information to provide users with the best entity choices across multiple labels, thereby simplifying the entity selection process. The system comprises several components, including pre-extraction, filtering, adaptation, re-ranking, and real-time interfaces, each playing a crucial role in the contextual named entity retrieval system. The effectiveness of the system was validated through user studies and numerical assessments on diverse datasets, demonstrating its efficacy across various domains, including semantic search applications.

This article presents a concise overview of the tilings package, a collection of tools for creating temporaldisplays in R. We demonstrate how these displays can be connected to other plots and maintain consistency with the user's workflow, and provide specific examples of effectively using temporal displays in real-world scenarios.

Recent advancements in Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks (H-GNN) have led to their successful application in modeling complex relationships within Electronic Health Records. However, one major limitation of current H-GNN models is their inability to utilize additional information such as patient identities and institution affiliations when creating predictive models, using aggregation functions that are inherently non-linear and sensitive to node degree. Furthermore, many of these models are unable to scale to large real-world record sets due to computational constraints. In this paper, we present a new H-GNN model called PGNN that addresses these limitations using a linear combination of node features that incorporates patient and institution identity information, featuring a reduced computational complexity of O(N^2L). We evaluate our model's performance on two benchmark datasets, demonstrating superior predictive accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art models. The source code for our model is made available publicly at https://github.com/asharakeh/PGNN.

We investigated electrolyte properties near a softly charged surface using molecular dynamics simulations of a monovalent 1-1 zwitterionic electrolyte confined between two plates and two types of disordered, non-charged surfaces. We found that as ionic size increased, the structure and dynamics of the electrolyte became more similar to a coexisting macroscopic and microscopic phase separation observed in the system between charged plates. We attributed these findings to a shift in electrolyte properties from a bulk-like state to a surface-like state due to increased charge exclusion. Moreover, we discovered that the observed phase coexistence tends to be suppressed when the surface charge density is too low or too diffuse.

Software engineering researchers have been exploring the effectiveness of
BERT, a pre-trained language model, in processing software text for purposes
such as identifying project summaries and requirement documents. Yet, no study
has evaluated BERT's performance relative to other neural network-based
approaches like fastText and ELMo on a broad scale. Our research aimed to fill
this knowledge gap by employing a diverse dataset of project summaries to
evaluate BERT, ELMo, and fastText using the same feature extraction pipeline,
and similar evaluation metrics. Our results show that BERT significantly outperformed
El'net solutions in feature extraction, with its extracted features resulting in
a cross-validation accuracy of 85.54% and ROC-AUC score of 0.8704. While BERT's
performance surpassed that of ELMo and fastText, our analysis of the extracted
features revealed that the three models focused on different sets of words.

This paper explores energy-efficient strategies within a multi-user, multi-relay system where both relay scheduling and power allocation are considered to minimize the total energy consumption of cooperating nodes while maintaining the quality of service for all users. To address this complex problem, the proposed solution assumes a specific bandwidth allocation and applies a majorization approach to optimize power allocation. Subsequently, the paper presents a relay scheduling method that is independent of power allocation. Notably, the derived results exhibit a significant reduction in energy consumption compared to conventional methods, with even greater efficiency when the bandwidth can be freely allocated.

Utilizing scanning tunneling spectroscopy, researchers have discovered YS (Y and Si) or spin-polarized X (X = Bi, Pb, and Yb) auto-localized states near magnetic adatoms or dimers on the (100) surface of silicon. By conducting density functional theory calculations that incorporate spin-orbit coupling, they determined that, unlike the case of non-cooperative magnetic coupling, variations in magnetic dimer orientation significantly influence peak positions, widths, and propagation patterns. The observed multiple peak formations per magnetic dimer or atomic structure variation on silicon can serve as a spin susceptibility measure in experimental studies.

The NA62 experiment at CERN has completed an analysis of data from a run in 2018 for a specific decay process. With a data set of 0.37 in magnitude for the decay of $K^+$ into $\pi^+$ and a pair of muons, they established an upper limit of $BR(K^+ \to \pi^+ \nu \bar{\nu}) < 5.1 \times 10^{-10}$ at 90% confidence, which is about four standard deviations away from the expected value based on the $K^+$ mass and semileptonic decay rate. This result is in line with the expectations from the Standard Model.

This paper presents a novel down-sampling technique to enhance the accuracy of self-registration for LIDAR point clouds, particularly effective to some extent in traffic environments characterized by static and dynamic objects. By down-sampling the cloud and retaining points with significant elevation changes, we introduce the Cluster-Reflector-Cluster (CRC) point sampling method. CRC takes advantage of this filtered point cloud to significantly reduce data without compromising accuracy, enabling the initial registration of LIDAR data. Our CRC approach achieves this without any external references, global optimization or high-computational radio features, demonstrating its efficiency on real-world data highlighting dynamic objects and static environments.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to impressive performance in various applications using deep learning methods for satellite image analysis. Despite their success, these methods face several satellite-specific challenges, such as dealing with fragmented and isolated land parcels, which necessitate significant labeled data for accurate classification. To address this need, we introduce a semi-supervised image segmentation approach that combines local and global characteristics to identify land use patterns, even with limited annotations. This technique also considers the intricacies of satellite imaging by designing an efficient unet-like architecture. Our method treats input patch-wise image segmentation as a multi-task problem by implementing two functions: one assigns labels to individual images, and the other performs segmentation using average pixel values. To enhance this process, we incorporate transportation mapping and develop a specialized loss function. Our method's efficiency is demonstrated by its ability to process high-resolution images (such as PLotting $512 \times 512$) with minimal computational requirements. Evaluation on real-world datasets reveals that our approach achieves state-of-the-art land use segmentation accuracy using a fraction of the labels required by fully supervised methods, achieving land use fractional area accuracy of 91.4% using only 1% of labels compared to fully supervised supervised land use segmentation at 93.2% using 100% labels.

The dynamics of electron redistribution in ferromagnetic metals like nickel under high-intensity laser pulses is investigated down to the attosecond timescale. Attosecond transient absorption changes and sublinear absorption patterns observed at elevated fluences are explained by distinct electron trajectories driven by laser pulses of varying intensities. A theoretical model accounting for electron motion reveals two distinct electron groups with unique time frames for absorption resulting in distinct absorption patterns. These distinct electron groups correspond to primary and secondary electron emissions which converge at different point-in-time ($t_0$ and $t_{0s}$) respectively. The initial (primary) electron group absorbs the laser pulse at the same time as the lattice (at $t_0$), whereas a much weaker (secondary) electron group emerges at $t_{0s}$ (around 170 fs after $t_0$) due to inter-electron collisions. It has been found that the latter ($t_{0s}$) is the point-in-time relevant for describing nonlinear absorption at high fluences, which is also supported by experimental data. Moreover, it has been found that the time-evolution of electron distribution in nickel is similar to that of liquid mercury, suggesting that the electron dynamics in nickel can be treated as a deconfining electron liquid.

Adversarial attacks have long been a major threat to deep neural networks and pose a significant risk to applications utilizing such models. To counter these attacks, generative adversarial networks are often utilized as a form of data protection mechanism by generating reconstructed data from corrupted input. Presently, the most effective countermeasures against adversarial noise involve both high-capacity gan models and training on extensive datasets of poisoned data. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel approach called Diagnose-and-Fit, which uses gan to tackle adversarial attacks in deep neural networks by fitting the gan on only a limited portion of a dataset already diagnosed as clean. Furthermore, we introduce a pioneering method called Gated-GAN, which controls the capacity of gan by regulating its internal data distribution, thereby preventing overfitting. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to state-of-the-art gan models, which yield superior robustness and reduced overfitting risk compared to existing methods, as validated on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets against various types of poisoning attacks.

A widely accepted method for segmenting multiple sclerosis lesions is supervised learning, commonly used by neurologists to divide MRI scans into healthy and affected areas. However, most datasets are limited to a single hospital's data, making it challenging to apply learned segmentation rules to scans from other institutions. A recent approach to overcome this limitation involves using experience replay, an unsupervised method developed to improve segmentation accuracy when training models with limited labeled data. Our study found that experience replay significantly improves lesion segmentation when training models with Experience-level annotations from a single hospital and then testing them on data from multiple institutions. Notably, this technique resulted in an increase of more than 10 points in the dice similarity coefficient compared to conventional supervised learning methods.

A modified comparison of metrics has been developed, primarily based on the concept of optimal transport. This is done by first introducing a proxy metric for each OT distance that is both highly correlated with it and continuity guaranteed. As a result, this enables a broader application of the properties associated with the OT distance, without direct reliance on it. Additionally, under specific assumptions, this setup can be used to extend continuity to a closed-loop case.

Hybrid models that combine data-driven and domain knowledge often require adjustments to balance these components to achieve optimal performance. In this paper, we present evidence that a straightforward mix of these expertise components exhibits complementary properties, leading to robust and efficient model designs. Our experiments with both synthetic and real-world problems in statistical analysis and reinforcement learning demonstrate that combining expertise components leads to superior performance, greater data efficiency, and more consistent outcomes. These findings are validated across multiple scenarios and further reveal that the benefits of hybrid models scale linearly with the extent of domain knowledge involved. Our results suggest that hybrid models can be an effective strategy for integrating knowledge into machine learning without necessitating extensive adjustments.

The formation of molecular cores and massive stars is a complex process, intertwined with core growth and fragmentation. To examine the relationship between core mass and stellar mass, we analyzed data from the core mass function and stellar mass function, assuming they follow power-law distributions with the same exponent $\alpha$. Using constraints from observations and theoretical calculations of core and stellar mass distributions, we determined the values of core and stellar mass, as well as the exponent $\alpha$, thereby calculating the ratio of stellar mass to core mass, $M_*$/$M_{core}$. Our results show that the growth of molecular cores and stellar masses follow similar patterns, characterized by a power-law distribution, with a calculated exponent $\alpha$ equal to 1.45. This value helps predict a $M_*$/$M_{core}$ ratio of approximately 16, with a corresponding uncertainty of a factor of two. This relationship between core and stellar mass is a crucial factor in determining the influence of core mass on stellar mass. This relationship also allows us to estimate the average stellar mass, $\langle M_*\rangle$, as a function of the average core mass, $\langle M_{core}\rangle$, and the exponent $\alpha$. This prediction implies that more massive cores can produce more massive stars. This relationship between core and stellar mass is a fundamental aspect of core collapse mass function derivation. This work may be further extended to derive the stellar initial mass function by combining the core mass function with the core formation rate. This approach may

Researchers anticipate identifying approximately 25-50 candidateincidentally detected black holes through microlensing beyond 2020. A recent study presents a comprehensive method to interpret microlensing events that are consistent with a stellar origin. By utilizing this method, it's estimated that around 1 to 20 microlensing events can be attributed to primordial black holes, assuming an average mass of 30 solar masses. Only one of these candidates would have a post-merger mass within the previously proposed window for a 2.5 solar mass LHC merger product. Nevertheless, our analysis suggests that stellar imprints can account for the majority of the observed microlensing events, leaving only a small likelihood of identifying a primordial black hole mass through microlensing.

We investigate the polar symmetry-planning problem, a challenge of arranging non-linear (polyhedral) objects in three-dimensional space with given spatial limitations. Our study focuses on the general case where object and space geometry is identical, except for size. The problem has connections to the polar symmetry of crystalline structures and frustrated systems. Through our analysis, we identify two new types of frustrated polar crystalline phases that appear when the packing density exceeds a certain threshold (greater than 0.5). One phase features an alternating polar direction trend that is consistent around a point; the other exhibits inconsistent trends based on which point is considered. We used computational methods to study this problem and confirmed the existence of these phases through group-theoretical analysis.

Pretrained language models excel at various NLP tasks by learning to associate
special tokens with the context, however the intricate meaning of these tokens
leads to inconsistent performance across tasks and contexts. We investigate the
effect of token representation on task-specific results by focusing on [MASK] and
STARSPACE tokens. Our research indicates that current models do not effectively
capture the essence of these tokens and therefore fail to optimize task performance 
appropriately. To address this limitation, we introduce new sets of special tokens 
for specific semantic domains and demonstrate the positive impact on model outcomes 
when integrated into the pretraining process. Our fine-tuned models achieve notable 
boosts in conversational understanding, particularly in the evaluation of conversational 
reasoning, with a notable improvement of 10.3% in F1-score in the SciADe v2 subtask.

For decades, metric learning has been a cornerstone of machine learning, enabling effective similarity comparisons between vectors. Traditionally, similarity functions like Euclidean distance, cosine similarity, or normalized dot product have been chosen without consideration for their metric learning capabilities. Recent research has demonstrated the benefits of metric learning when adding new elements to a dataset. To address this, a novel network architecture, the Analytic Metric Learning via Geometry-inspired Neural Networks (AGN), was designed to optimize similarity functions efficiently. AGN was tested on various network designs and learned metrics, as well as on diverse datasets including text, image, and tabular data. The results showed AGN performs better than existing methods on additions to a set, while its wall-clock time is significantly faster. Specifically, AGN is 2-6 times faster than conventional networks and 10-150 times faster than methods not utilizing learned metrics.

Our analysis investigates the relationship between angular velocity distributions in solid-like and liquid states, specifically focusing on the angular velocities of molecules in a binary mixture that exhibits thermodynamic scaling characteristics, as demonstrated by data from molecular dynamics simulations. Utilizing a simplified theoretical model, we calculate the ratio of the solid to liquid values of the integral of the angular velocity distribution, and find that it adheres to the principles of thermodynamic scaling when the components of the mixture have disparate sizes. This theoretical model also predicts that the rescaled dimensionless values of the calculated property should display time-stability, an observation that is corroborated by our molecular dynamics simulations results.

Our study focuses on the impact of negation words on natural language inference tasks, revealing distinct effects based on word category (content, modality, or negation) and context. We observed that all categories of negation negatively affect model performance in NLI tasks, with modality negation having a marginally lesser impact. Notably, using BERTscorer with category-aware embeddings significantly improved results for NLI on the BERTscorer dataset, but had a negative effect on standard NLI datasets, implying that such embeddings are specific to NLI tasks requiring negation modeling. We analyzed category embeddings from BERT and found that they align with their semantic categories, are stable across NLI datasets, and are consistent with human perceptions of negation categories. We also demonstrated the utility of category-aware embeddings in modeling inductive NLI reasoning, where predictions on unseen instances with similar negation words but differing contexts were made.

The sequential nature of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models means they rely on previous words to predict future words, which can lead to suboptimal translations when processing is complete but words are still relevant in the context. To overcome this, we propose an attention mechanism that allows these models to "look ahead" and use post-position contextual information. Our specific implementation, called LookAheadAttention, incorporates additional neural layers that take into account not only existing hidden states but also a representation derived from a specialized Transformer layer. We have evaluated this mechanism in both the attention-based and encoder-decoder settings and observed a notable increase in BLEU scores for the WMT 14 English to German task.

This note revisits connections, curvature, and weights within symplectic geometry,
focusing particularly on cotangent bundles. By examining underlying properties,
our analysis indicates that expressing curvature weights in $\lambda_\mu$ form is
preferable; this expression is naturally derived from connections, yielding specific
characterizations in both cases of a Lagrangian submanifold and within Lagrangian
twisted structures.

A thorough analysis is performed on the impact of a specific parameter, referred to as 'c', which measures how strongly the left- and right- hand sides of a conformal field theory interact with each other in a symmetric environment. This study evaluates thermal entropy changes and confirms an established 12-minute rule. Other notable results include the verification of a previously theoretical 12-minute rule for the thermal entropy of specific types of conformal field theories and the development of two new inequalities that restrict the range of possible values for specific types of entropy in a symmetric environment. These results were obtained through the creation of specific types of entropy in a symmetric environment and were found using advanced mathematical concepts, including the properties of specific types of functions and their values. These concepts were applied to the construction of a symmetric environment, which allows for the calculation of specific types of entropy in a symmetric environment and was found using advanced mathematical concepts, which relate to the properties of specific types of functions and their values.

This research presents an innovative approach to computing the Black-Scholes formula of Asian options by utilizing one finite and two distinct forms of the single Laplace transform. Our method requires the computation of only three Laplace parameters which can be efficiently determined through an elementary search algorithm. Our findings demonstrate that the two novel forms of the single Laplace transform lead to significantly reduced computational complexity in generating a pre-calculated look-up table, when compared to the existing body-of-literature methods. Moreover, the linear search algorithm to determine the three optimal Laplace parameters results in a computational complexity of O(n), where n represents the number of grid points in the domain of the volatility parameter. Our results also showcase the effectiveness of numerical differentiation and interpolation techniques in producing highly accurate numerical results for the Black-Scholes formula of Asian options.

The Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope has detected a diffuse gamma-ray background across the entire sky, with its spectrum remaining a mystery despite multiple attempts to explain it. A new research paper suggests that the diffuse background can be attributed to the clustering of galaxies within galaxy groups and clusters, with the gamma-ray emission resulting from the acceleration of electrons within turbulent hot gas. The process involves the conversion of cosmic rays into secondary electrons and positrons that, in turn, trigger gamma-ray emission through Inverse Compton interactions with the surrounding cosmic microwave background radiation and reprocessed cosmic ray photons. The study considers the interactions between these particles and radiation within the dark matter halos of galaxy groups and clusters using simplified models, with results indicating that the observed diffuse background can indeed be explained through this galactic cluster medium. The calculated spectrum and photon production rate through Inverse Compton interactions with the cosmic microwave background radiation match Fermi observations, with adjustments to model parameters needed to account for gamma-ray emission resulting from the collision of cosmic rays with pre-existing photons within turbulent plasmas. The study also offers potential avenues to further investigate the spectrum, with implications for our understanding of galaxy formation and the galaxy-halo connection.

Inflation models with sharp features in their potential or sound-horizon scale oscillations leave behind distinct non-Gaussian signatures in the cosmic microwave background. This paper delves into the theoretical framework of these features, focusing on their relationship to the bispectrum and how this impact the constraints on $f_{\rm NL}$ when using Planck data and future experiments like CMB-S4 and PIPER.

This research proposes an innovative method to produce engaging captions for the visual outputs of sophisticated computer vision models, except these captions aren't tied to specific image inputs. Instead, they serve as a way to understand the underlying representations learned by these models. The suggested approach, called Latent Visual Semantic Explainer (LaViSE), analyzes and interprets the structural composition of convolutional neural networks through backpropagation and adaptive image manipulation. LaViSE generates natural language descriptions that accurately represent the focuses and characteristics of the networks' internal representations. In addition, LaViSE enables users to adjust the level of abstraction and the volume of output descriptions. It also allows users to develop a deeper comprehension of the networks' structural composition and the relationships between different representations. LaViSE can be applied to various computer vision lossless compression and post-hoc analysis techniques.

Inspired by the emerging role of 2D materials in high-temperature superconductors, we
investigate the 1D materials Ba$_{2}$Black$_{2}$, which exhibit strong similarities to
the 2D BaBlack$_{2}$ family, known for high-temperature superconductors. We employ
series expansion methods to study the 1D materials up to very high temperatures, and
our results for the 1D materials match closely with predictions made by SU(2) and large-N
models in the context of the 2D materials. Our findings indicate that understanding the
1D materials can provide valuable insights into the properties of the 2D materials and may
even contribute to discovering new superconductors at high temperatures.

To address the growing issue of missing HIV-positive individuals in sub-Saharan Africa, researchers have been exploring the use of spatial analytics. A critical challenge facing affected countries is identifying strategies to locate these individuals and encouraging them to attend healthcare facilities. An innovative method involves utilizing travel time to healthcare facilities as a key factor in an incentive-based approach. Through the analysis of South African township data, researchers discovered that familiarity with travel time to HIV care facilities influences an individual's decision to undergo treatment for HIV. Furthermore, average appointment times, as reported by taxi drivers, significantly predict the local prevalence of undiagnosed HIV-positive individuals. These findings imply that accessible travel time information can motivate individuals to attend healthcare facilities, whereas sharing appointment times among a network of trusted contacts may further enhance treatment rates.

The creation of a metastable skyrmion lattice is demonstrated by rapidly decreasing the magnetic field applied to a palladium/scenium/bismuth trilayer with a fixed unidirectional coercive field. Observing the transformation from a stable to a metastable skyrmion lattice under a positive magnetic field enables the stabilization of the metastable phase down to zero magnetic field where it undergoes a phase transition into a laminated structure comprising stripes of stripe phases. Notably, the metastable skyrmion lattice undergoes transformations similar to those seen under negative magnetic fields but in reverse, indicating a second-order phase transition under negative magnetic fields and a first-order phase transition under positive magnetic fields.

We introduce a novel class of singular ARMA models based on the concept of partial rank, and establish certain fundamental properties. This idea has far-reaching implications in the analysis of high-dimensional dynamic factor models, and the theoretical results derived here are used to prove consistency and convergence rates for these models in practical applications. Our theoretical findings are illustrated with examples and a practical example is demonstrated in the context of macroeconomic data analysis, specifically singular ARMA models for high-dimensional macroeconomic variables in the United States, where we recover the common factors and a low-rank ARMA structure for these variables.

The primary objective of this research is to delve into the characteristics of the Moreau proximal mapping in relation to the solutions of certain problems, specifically those that involve the satisfaction of multiple equilibrium conditions. We demonstrate that under certain, broadly applicable conditions, the points to which the proximal mapping converges after repeated application are also solutions to these equilibrium problems, thus potentially serving as metrics for measuring the progress of algorithms designed to solve such problems. A specific set of conditions has been identified that ensures the convergence of proximal points to actual solutions to the equilibrium problem in question. These conditions are analogous to those that define strict anti-equilibrium points in relation to the Georgescu-Pinheiro time-distance function, thus establishing a connection between two distinct methods for solving equilibrium problems and highlighting the potential for duplication between these two approaches.

Deep learning models frequently rely on deterministic output, which makes it challenging to assess their uncertainty level. Employing Bayesian methods allows us to quantify uncertainty stemming from model constraints and data limitations. While uncertainty estimation is typically confined to model output, certain applications require uncertainty bounds on individual data elements. This paper explores techniques for obtaining posterior probability distributions of image pixels under a mean-square error loss criterion. We examine theoretical approaches and propose a simplified posterior sampling method for practical implementation. The proposed method is evaluated on two tasks: predicting Gaussian random fields and replicating well-known image denoising models using the Bayesian residual network framework. The study compares the performance of these models with their non-Bayesian counterparts, considering computational efficiency in the evaluation.

The geophysical alpha-dynamo must consider all turbulent effects within its mathematical model in order to accurately predict magnetic field generation. This is particularly significant for stellar and solar systems where geo-dynamics play a crucial role, and neglecting certain turbulent effects can lead them to enter the magnetohydrodynamic instability zone. By incorporating all turbulent effects into the model, our research shows how the geo-dynamo can generate persistent and stable magnetic fields even without external forces. This is achieved through an in-depth analysis using the Babcock-Orekhov cycle mechanism and a multi-layered model that takes into account various dynamo processes, including the small-scale geostrophic and pseudo-geostrophic instabilities. Our research provides a theoretical framework for understanding magnetic field dynamics and offers a possible explanation for the magnetic fields observed in certain stars.

This research reveals the movement of both neutral and molecular gases within the galaxy under conditions similar to those in the early universe. The movement of gas is detected in the core and disk areas but is blocked by a dense gas layer in the disk's mid-point. It's found that the overall flow of molecular gas in the core is 420 cubic centimeters per year. The movement pattern of the gas is explained by using a simplified model of two separate gas clouds.
